item.title: 'I Sent Money by Mistake': The Mobile Money Send-Back Scam
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: A message says money was sent to you by mistake and asks you to return it. Learn how this trick works, how to check, and what to do if you already paid.
item.content:encoded:
Your phone buzzes. A message says money has arrived. A minute later, a call or another text says, "Sorry, that was my mistake, please send it back. I am in trouble." You want to be kind. Most of us would. That kindness is exactly what this trick uses, so first, know this: if you fell for it, or almost did, you are not foolish.

The short answer

Do not send anything back because of a message alone. Messages can be faked, and a real sender can get their money back through their own operator. First check your own balance through your operator's official channel, not through the text. If the money is not really in your balance, there is nothing to return.

  • Never give your PIN to anyone, for any reason.
  • Do not act on a text that only looks like it came from customer service.
  • Do not rush. Scammers need you to hurry.
  • If a real sender made a mistake, they can ask their own operator for a reversal.
  • Report the number and keep the messages.

How the send-back trick works

TCRA's Consumer Consultative Council (TCRA-CCC) described this trick in Tanzanian press in 2017 (The Citizen, 30 January 2017, updated in March 2021). It goes like this:

  1. A text arrives that says money was sent to your account by mistake. Nothing may have been sent at all. The text only looks like a real mobile money alert.
  2. A second text follows. It is made to look like it comes from the network's customer service. It asks you to return the money.
  3. If you send your own money, it is gone. The person at the other end is a scammer, not someone who made a mistake.

The council urged users not to respond or act on such messages, even when the number looks familiar. Its advice was to call that number from a different phone to confirm who is really writing.

The trick is old, and TCRA has run public campaigns against mobile money fraud in later years too. For example, TCRA's page of 4 August 2022 asks people to check both the message and the number that asks for money before any transaction. We do not claim here that the trick is more or less common today than it used to be, because we could not confirm current numbers for this particular scam.

Checks to make before you send anything

Stop and run through this short list. It takes two minutes and can save you a week's wages.

  1. Check your balance the official way. Use your operator's own menu, app or customer service, not a link or number given in the message. If the money is not in your balance, the message was fake.
  2. Look at the sender. A real alert comes from your operator's usual sender name. A message from an ordinary phone number that talks like a bank is a warning sign.
  3. Never share your PIN. No operator, agent or "customer service" needs it to take money back.
  4. Call the person from a different phone if you know them, as the council advised. If you do not know them, do not send money.
  5. Tell the sender to use their own operator. If someone really sent money by mistake, ask them to contact their operator and ask for a reversal. We do not print operator codes in this post, because we could not check them on official pages. Ask your operator for the current process.
  6. Sleep on it if you can. A real mistake can wait an hour. A scam cannot.

The TCRA campaign page gives similar advice in plain words: never send money through your mobile phone to someone you do not know, and examine the message and the number before completing a transaction.

What real operators do, and what scammers do

This table shows patterns. It is a guide, not a guarantee.

A real operator or senderA scammer
Lets you check your balance in the official menu or appTells you to trust the text and not check
Never asks for your PINAsks for your PIN "to cancel the mistake"
Handles reversals through its own processAsks you to send the money to a personal number
Lets you take your timeSays it is urgent and someone is in trouble
Does not call to announce prizes or bonusesCalls to say you have won something

On that last point, The Citizen reported in 2017 that Vodacom Tanzania said it does not call customers to tell them about M-Pesa bonus payments, and never asks customers for their M-Pesa password before paying promotional winnings. That is one operator's statement from 2017, but the habit is a good one to keep with any operator.

Fake prize calls and fake customer-service messages

The same trick has cousins. In the 2017 report, callers told people they had won money in a promotion or an M-Pesa bonus. TCRA's 2022 campaign says that if someone calls to say you won a lottery you never entered, you should not respond.

Hang up. A real prize does not need you to pay first, share a PIN or send "a small fee". You cannot win a promotion you never joined.

TCRA also says not to follow instructions from unknown callers whose identity you cannot confirm. If a caller claims to be from your operator, end the call and ring your operator through the number you already trust. TCRA's campaign page says you can reach your service provider by dialling 100.

If you sell goods and get payment texts, see our post on fake mobile money payment messages for sellers. For voice calls that sound like family, see AI voice and video scams.

If you already sent money

First, be kind to yourself. Scams like this are designed by people who do this daily. Your feeling of shame is normal, and it is the thing the scammer counts on to keep you quiet. Do not let it stop you from acting.

Act as soon as you can:

  1. Contact your operator. TCRA says to send your complaint to your service provider first, in writing. Tell them what happened and give the time, the amount and the number you sent to.
  2. Go to a police station. TCRA's FAQ advises reporting fraud there to get an RB number and an investigator. Take the messages and your transaction record.
  3. Report the number by SMS to 15040. TCRA's FAQ says to send the word UTAPELI followed by the number. Its 2022 campaign page says to send "Fraud". The pages differ, so follow the automated reply you get and check tcra.go.tz for the current wording.
  4. Escalate if needed. If your operator does not answer within 30 days, or you are not satisfied with the reply, TCRA says you can complain to it. Its toll-free line is 0800008272.
  5. Keep the evidence. Do not delete the texts or call logs.

We cannot promise that you will get your money back. We can say that reporting helps: TCRA's campaign page says reported numbers are investigated by law enforcement.

TCRA's FAQ also says you can dial *106# to confirm that your SIM registration is complete. If you think someone is misusing your identity, follow what the screen shows.

Common questions

What if someone really did send me money by mistake?

Check your balance in the official channel first. If the money is there, ask the sender to contact their own operator for a reversal. We have not checked what Tanzanian law says about keeping money sent in error, so we give no legal view. Ask your operator or the police if you are unsure.

The message used my name. Is it real?

Not necessarily. Scammers can learn names from public posts or from other leaks. A name does not prove a message is real.

Can I call the number that texted me?

If you do, use a different phone, as the council advised, and never give a PIN. A better option is to check your balance first and say nothing until you know.

Does a message from a number I know count as proof?

No. TCRA-CCC said not to act even when the number looks familiar. Phone numbers can be copied or a friend's phone can be misused. Confirm by calling the person on another line.

What to do next

  1. Choose one rule today: "I check my balance in the official menu before I send anything back."
  2. Tell your family, especially older relatives, that nobody ever needs a PIN.
  3. Save your operator's customer-care contact from its official page, so you can reach it fast.
  4. If you were caught, report it, and do not carry the shame alone.

One careful pause can protect your hard-earned money, and a short pause is something anyone can learn.

Sources and further reading

  • Frequent asked questions on customer and consumer affairs, TCRA
  • TCRA launches campaign to curb online fraud, TCRA (4 August 2022)
  • Council alarmed by wave of mobile money thefts, The Citizen (30 January 2017, updated March 2021)

item.title: A One-Page Marketing Plan for a Small Business on a Small Budget
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Build a one-page marketing plan with one goal, one customer, two channels, a small TSh budget and a monthly check. Simple steps and a table you can copy.
item.content:encoded:
Many small owners try everything at once. A poster on Monday, a social media page on Tuesday, a flyer on Wednesday. By the end of the month they are tired, the money is gone, and they cannot say what worked.

You can do better with less. A marketing plan does not need to be a thick document. One page is enough, and a page you actually follow is worth more than a long plan in a drawer.

The short answer

A one-page plan has five parts: one goal you can measure, one kind of customer, two ways of reaching them, a small budget with a weekly routine, and a monthly check where you change only one thing. Write it in a notebook or on one sheet of paper and keep it where you work.

  • Pick one goal with a number and a date.
  • Name the customer you most want to reach.
  • Choose only two channels that you can keep up every week.
  • Set a budget you can lose without harm, and say how you will measure it.
  • Review once a month and change one thing at a time.

Why a short plan beats a big one

Business Queensland, an Australian government service, gives plain advice in its guide to writing a marketing plan: "Don't try to do everything at once." It says to spread the work out according to the time, skills and people you have. It also says to test ideas with friendly customers before you commit, and to check regularly what is working.

That advice fits a one-person shop as well as it fits a company. We use the Queensland guide for its method only. None of its figures or rules apply to Tanzania, and all the TSh amounts below are examples we made up.

If you have not yet found out who your customers are, do that first. Our post on how to know your customers takes about a week and costs nothing.

Step 1: Write one goal you can measure

"Get more customers" is not a goal. You cannot tell when you have reached it.

Business Queensland describes a "SMART" goal. It is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and has a time limit. In plain words: say what you want, give it a number, make sure it is possible for you, make sure it helps the business, and give it a date.

Some examples of the shape of a good goal:

  • "Get 15 new customers to buy at least once in the next three months."
  • "Have 8 customers ask for a repeat order by the end of December."
  • "Collect 20 phone numbers of people who want to hear about new stock by the end of March."

Notice that these ask for customers and actions, not for a promise of money. You cannot control how much people spend. You can control how many people you speak to and how you follow up.

Choose one goal. If you have three, you have none.

Step 2: Name your customer and pick two channels

Write one sentence that describes the customer you want most. For example: "Mothers who live within a short walk of my shop and buy school items." The more clearly you can picture them, the easier the next choice becomes.

Business Queensland suggests choosing target groups by how large they are, how much they could bring in, and how easy they are to reach. If you cannot reach a group cheaply, it is probably not the right one to start with.

Now pick two channels. A channel is just a way to reach people. Some common low-cost choices:

ChannelGood forCost and effort
A clear sign or painted board at your shopPeople who pass byOne-time cost, little weekly work
Word of mouth and thanking customersPeople who already trust youFree, but needs a kind habit
A WhatsApp status or a social media pagePeople who already have your number or follow youFree to post, needs a regular time slot
A flyer or notice at a place your customer visitsA local areaPrinting cost, needs permission in some places
A simple phone call or message to past buyersRepeat salesFree apart from airtime

Pick two that match your customer. If your customers are mothers near your shop, a sign and word of mouth may beat a social media page. If your customers are young people who scroll all day, a regular post may work better. Do not choose a channel only because your neighbour uses it.

Why two? Because you have limited hours. One channel done well each week beats five done once.

Step 3: Set a small budget and a weekly routine

Start with an amount you could lose without hurting your family or your stock money. It may be small, and that is fine.

Here is an example. All the numbers are made up. Say you set aside TSh 30,000 a month:

  • TSh 15,000 for printing 50 small notices
  • TSh 10,000 for airtime and data to send messages and post
  • TSh 5,000 kept back to test one new idea

That adds up to TSh 30,000. Check the total whenever you write a budget, because mistakes here are common.

Do not copy these amounts. Use your own figures. The point is to write them down before you spend, so you can compare the plan with what really happened.

Now add a routine. Time is a cost too. The Queensland guide says each action should have timing, a person responsible and a way of measuring it. In a one-person business, the person is you. For example:

  • Monday, 15 minutes: Post one photo and one useful sentence about a product.
  • Wednesday, 15 minutes: Message three past customers to say thanks and ask if they need anything.
  • Saturday, 10 minutes: Write in your notebook how many people asked about the business and how they heard of it.

Forty minutes a week is something most owners can keep up. A routine you can keep is better than a big push that stops after two weeks.

Step 4: Put it on one page

Draw a table in your notebook or on a sheet of paper. Here is a sample you can copy. The details are an example only.

Part of the planYour answer (example)
Goal and date15 new customers who buy at least once by the end of January
My customerParents who live near the shop and buy school items
Channel 1A painted sign and 50 notices at the school gate and the church board
Channel 2A weekly photo and message on WhatsApp status
Monthly budgetTSh 30,000 (TSh 15,000 printing, TSh 10,000 airtime, TSh 5,000 test)
Weekly routineMonday post, Wednesday messages, Saturday count
How I measureAsk every new customer "How did you hear about us?" and tally the answers
Review dateThe last Sunday of each month

Ask yourself two questions about the page. Can I do all of this with the time I really have? Can I measure the goal without special tools? If the answer to either is no, make the plan smaller.

Measuring does not need software. A tally of tick marks in a notebook is enough. The key is to ask each new customer how they found you, and to write it down at once.

Step 5: Check results every month and change one thing

Business Queensland suggests reviewing the plan regularly and asking what is working and what has changed in the market. Its guide mentions checking each quarter. For a small shop with a small budget, a short monthly look is easier to keep.

On your review day, answer these questions:

  1. How many new customers did I get, and how did they hear about me?
  2. Did I do my weekly routine, or did I skip it? Why?
  3. Did I stay inside my budget?
  4. Which channel brought more people?
  5. What is one thing I will change next month?

Change only one thing. If you change the message, the channel and the price at once, you will not know which change mattered.

Be patient and honest. Some months will show little. That does not always mean the plan has failed. Sometimes it means the customer needs more time, or the message is unclear. We cannot promise any result, and nobody honest can. What a plan gives you is a clear way to learn from what you try.

Common questions

Do I need a big budget to market my business?

No. Many useful actions cost only time and airtime, such as thanking customers, asking for referrals and posting regularly. Spend only what you can afford to lose.

Which two channels should I choose?

Choose the two that your customer already uses and that you can keep up every week. Your own notes from customer chats are the best guide.

How long before I see results?

It varies, and nobody can promise a date. Give a channel at least a few weeks of steady effort before you judge it, and track how customers say they found you.

Should I pay someone to run my marketing?

Not at the start. Learn what works yourself first. If you later pay someone, you will know what to ask for. Be careful with anyone who promises sales or a top place in search results.

What to do next

  1. Write your one goal with a number and a date.
  2. Fill in the one-page table above using your own answers.
  3. Put a reminder for your monthly review on a calendar or phone.
  4. Keep going for three months before you decide the plan is not working.

You do not have to be a marketer to grow a business a step at a time. A plan this small is something you can start today.

Sources and further reading

  • Writing a marketing strategy and plan, Business Queensland
  • Customer focus, Business Queensland
  • Market research and competitive analysis, U.S. Small Business Administration

These pages come from Queensland, Australia and the United States. We used them for general method only, as checked in November 2026. Their programmes and rules do not apply to Tanzania.

item.title: Accepting Mobile Money in Your Business: Lipa Number Basics
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Learn why a merchant (Lipa) number is safer than a personal line, what Mixx by Yas asks for, how customers pay, and how to guard your till against scams.
item.content:encoded:
Many customers no longer carry much cash. They say "nitume" and expect to pay by phone. If your business can only receive money on your personal line, the shop money, your family money and your friends' messages all end up in one place. That is stressful and hard to track.

This post explains the merchant number idea, what one network asks for, and how to protect yourself. We could only confirm details for some networks, and we say clearly which ones.

The short answer

A merchant number, called a Lipa number, is a number made for business payments. Customers pay it, you get a message, and the payments are easier to separate from your personal money. Ask your network what you need, keep every payment in your cash book, and never hand over goods before you have checked the payment is real.

  • Use a merchant number instead of a personal line where your network offers one.
  • Be ready with your NIDA number. Some levels also ask for a TIN certificate and a business licence.
  • Check the payment on your own phone or portal, not on the customer's screen.
  • Report scam messages to your network and keep the evidence.
  • Ask the network about any charges. We do not quote fees because we could not confirm them.

What is a Lipa (merchant) number and how do customers pay it?

Lipa kwa simu means "pay by phone". A merchant registers with a mobile money network and gets a number that customers use to pay the business.

On its customer page, Mixx by Yas (the network that was formerly Tigo Pesa) says a customer can pay in two ways, as checked in November 2026:

With USSD (no app): dial 15001#, choose Lipa Kwa Simu, choose TanQR, enter the merchant's number, check the merchant details shown, then enter the PIN.

With the Mixx Super App: open the app, tap Pay, scan the merchant's QR code or choose Merchant and type the number, enter the amount, check the merchant details and enter the PIN.

Yas says on its FAQ page that payments can come from all networks. Menus change, so ask your network for the current steps before you teach your customers.

What do the networks ask for?

We opened the Mixx by Yas merchant page, as checked in November 2026. It lists documents by type of merchant:

Merchant typeWhat the page says you need
Low KYC (NIDA only)A fully registered Yas number and a NIN or NIDA ID
Full KYC (individual)The same, plus a valid TIN with certificate and a valid business licence
Companies and institutionsA company TIN, a company business licence, the certificate of incorporation, and an authorisation letter, with extra papers for limited companies and sole proprietors

KYC means "know your customer": the checks a network makes on who you are. The Yas FAQ says merchants must be registered and that it is typically one line per business. For registration, it says to contact Mixx by Yas.

The page also lists features: several business accounts under one number, instant SMS alerts to several phones, scheduled transfers to a bank account that it says are free, a web portal for sales reports, and the option to add authorised users. It says no refunds are processed without your approval. The page lists no merchant fees, but it links to terms we could not read here, so ask the network before you sign up.

If you still need a TIN or licence, see our post on registering a small business with BRELA, TIN and licence.

What about Vodacom M-Pesa, Airtel Money and HaloPesa?

We opened Vodacom's M-Pesa Business onboarding page. It is written for organisations. It says to email m-pesabusiness@Vodacom.co.tz, complete forms and KYC checks, and sign the Services Agreement. The team then creates the organisation account and a 6- or 7-digit short code linked to a bank account. The charging model is agreed during the review, so we cannot say what it costs.

We did not open an official merchant page for Airtel Money or HaloPesa, and we did not find Vodacom's route for an individual small trader. So we will not guess. Visit a shop or agent of your network, or its website, and ask three things: what documents, what charges, and how fast the money arrives.

How do I protect my till from fake messages?

A merchant number does not protect you from tricks. Sellers are targets because they hand over goods fast.

  • Do not rely on a screenshot or on the customer's phone. Look at your own SMS alert, your app or the portal.
  • Be careful with messages that arrive while the customer stands at your counter and look almost right but come from an ordinary number.
  • Never send money back "because I paid too much" until you have checked your own balance.
  • Never share your PIN or any code with anyone, including someone who says they work for the network.

TCRA advises the public never to send money to someone they do not know, not to click links they do not recognise, and to check a message and number before paying (TCRA, August 2022). TCRA also says to dial *106# to see the numbers registered under your national ID and to text the word "Fraud" to 15040 to report scam messages. The Yas FAQ gives the same instruction for fraud reports. Because networks may change the keyword, check your network's current advice.

If you or a customer sends money to the wrong number, the Yas FAQ says to call customer care on 100, and that a reversal request must be made within 30 minutes of the mistaken transaction.

How do I match mobile money to my cash book?

Every payment is money in. Each evening, add up your SMS alerts or the portal report and write the total in your cash book next to your cash sales. Our post on simple business records and a cash book shows the columns.

Then compare. Cash in your box plus the merchant balance should equal the book balance. Withdraw a fixed amount for yourself and write it as "owner took". Do not pay household bills straight from the business line without writing it down.

Fees are your job to find. Ask your network for the current tariff for receiving payments and for moving money out, and write the charges in the book as an expense. When you work out prices, include them. Our post on how to price your products explains how.

Common questions

Do I need a merchant number to accept mobile money?

You can receive money on a personal line, but then business and personal money mix and are hard to separate. Ask your network what it allows for businesses.

Can a customer on a different network pay me?

The Yas FAQ says payments can come from all networks. Ask when you register, and test with a small payment.

How do I know a payment is real?

Look at your own alert, app or portal. If you cannot see it there, treat it as not paid.

What does a merchant number cost?

We could not confirm any fee, so we give none. Ask your network for its current tariff in writing.

What to do next

  1. Decide which network most of your customers use.
  2. Collect your NIDA number, and your TIN and business licence if you have them.
  3. Ask the network what you need, what it charges and when the money reaches you.
  4. Teach everyone who serves customers to check payments on the business phone before giving goods.

A small step like this makes your business look more serious to customers, and it gives you clearer numbers every evening.

Sources and further reading

  • Lipa Kwa Simu for merchants, Mixx by Yas
  • Lipa Kwa Simu for consumers, Mixx by Yas
  • Consumer FAQs, Yas Tanzania
  • Business onboarding in Tanzania, Vodacom M-Pesa Business
  • TCRA launches campaign to curb online fraud, Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority

item.title: Admitted to Several Universities? How to Confirm Just One
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Selected by more than one university in Tanzania? Learn the one-confirmation rule, how the confirmation code works, and what to ask your university.
item.content:encoded:
Being selected by two or three universities feels like good news and a puzzle at the same time. You worked hard for this, and now the system asks you to choose. Take a breath. This post explains the rule, what the official documents say, and what to ask your university.

The short answer

If more than one university selects you, you may confirm your admission at only one of them. The Tanzania Commission for Universities (TCU) calls this the confirmation step. You confirm the programme and university you prefer most.

  • The TCU admission guidebook says applicants admitted in more than one institution must confirm the most preferred programme and institution.
  • TCU's technical system document says a code from TCU is used to confirm one institution only.
  • You can ask for that code through the online system of the university.
  • Follow the instructions in your university portal, because each university runs its own page.
  • Confirmation dates change every year, so check the current guidebook.

Why can you be selected by more than one university?

Universities select students for their own programmes, so two of them can both say yes to the same student. The official documents treat this as a normal case and give a rule for it: you keep one place in the end.

This is not a mistake and it is not a warning sign. Being selected twice means your results were strong enough for both. It only means one decision is now yours to make.

What is the one-confirmation rule?

Two official documents describe it. Both are TCU documents, and we opened both in November 2026.

The first is the Bachelor's Degree Admission Guidebook for 2026/2027. Its general rules say that applicants admitted in more than one institution must confirm their admission to the most preferred programme and institution.

The second is a technical document for university systems (the API specification, version 4.3, dated July 2021). It says each applicant with multiple selections shall use a TCU token or code to confirm selection to only one higher learning institution, and that the choice is also confirmed with TCU.

The second document is older and written for system developers, so we use it only to explain the idea. The guidebook for the current year is the document to trust for rules and dates.

TCU also publishes lists of applicants who were admitted more than once. Those lists contain students' names, so we do not link to them. Use your own university account to see your own status. The TCU notices page also showed a third round of lists for 2026/27, so a year can have more than two rounds.

Notice what the rule does not say. It does not say that your other offers are punished or that you will be blocked. It says to confirm one.

How does the confirmation code work?

The technical document describes a confirmation code. In plain words:

  1. You have more than one selection.
  2. You ask for a confirmation code through the online system of the university you want to join.
  3. The university passes that request to TCU.
  4. You use the code to confirm that one university.

We could not find a plain-language TCU page that shows the screens and buttons. The TCU guidebook gives the rule, not a click-by-click guide. So we do not describe any steps that we could not check. Screens and wording differ from one university to another.

What you can do is this. Log in to the online admission page of your preferred university. Look for the words "confirm" or "confirmation code" in your account. If you cannot find them, read the admission message that came with your selection, or contact the admissions office.

Never pay anyone for a code. The code comes through the university system. If a stranger on social media offers to "get your code", do not send money or share your password.

Confirmation windows in 2026/27, as an example

TCU gives dates for each admission year. The 2026/2027 guidebook lists two confirmation windows:

RoundAdmission announcedConfirmation window
First application window8 September 20268 to 21 September 2026
Second application window6 October 20266 to 19 October 2026

As checked in November 2026, both windows have already closed for this year. We show them only so you can see how the process works. The dates for your year will be different. Read the guidebook for your own admission year on the TCU website, and note that the guidebook says the earliest date for universities to open for 2026/27 was 19 October 2026.

If you are reading this in the middle of a window, do not wait for the last day. Websites are slower at the end of a rush, and a weak mobile network can cost you hours.

What if you miss the window or lose the code?

This part needs honesty. The guidebook does not tell applicants what happens to an unconfirmed selection. We found no official sentence that explains it, so we will not guess.

What we do know from the technical document is that the system has actions for an applicant who confirmed and then changes their mind. An applicant who had confirmed can unconfirm through the online system of the university, and an applicant can cancel or reject an admission the same way. Those details are about the university system, and the exact steps may differ.

If you think you missed a deadline or lost your code:

  • Contact the admissions office of the university where you want to study. The guidebook says questions about applications and admissions go to the institution you applied to.
  • Do it quickly, in writing if you can, and keep a copy of your message.
  • Keep your application number and index number ready.
  • Be calm and polite. Admissions staff handle many cases like yours.

Common questions

Can I confirm two universities to be safe?

No. The rule is one confirmation. Confirming the one you really want is the safe choice.

How do I choose between two universities?

Compare things you can check: the programme name, the fees, the place, the cost of living, and whether the university is registered. Our post on how to check if a university or college is registered in Tanzania helps with that last point. If money is a worry, read the loan rules before you decide, in our HESLB loan guide.

Does TCU confirm me directly?

The technical document says the confirmation is passed to TCU through the university system. The applicant works through the university page. Follow your university portal's instructions.

I was not selected anywhere. What now?

That is a different situation and there are real options. See Not selected for university yet? What you can do next.

Is it safe to share my code?

Treat it like a password. Only enter it on the official page of your university.

What to do next

  1. Read the current TCU admission guidebook for your admission year, especially the dates table and the general rules.
  2. Decide which programme and university you want most, and write down why. Talk to your family or a teacher you trust.
  3. Log in to that university's admission page and look for the confirmation option. Ask the admissions office if you cannot find it.
  4. Finish before the window closes, and keep a screenshot or message that shows you confirmed.

You earned this choice. Make it calmly, and confirm the place you want.

Sources and further reading

  • Bachelor's Degree Admission Guidebook for Holders of Secondary School Qualifications 2026/2027, Tanzania Commission for Universities
  • Public Notices, Tanzania Commission for Universities
  • API Specification Documentation v4.3 (July 2021), TCU Undergraduate Admission System

item.title: AI Voice and Video Scams: How to Check Before You Send Money
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: A call that sounds like your child or your boss can be fake. Learn five checks that still work when the voice sounds real, and what to do if you paid.
item.content:encoded:
Your phone rings late in the evening. The voice is crying. It sounds like your daughter, or your brother, and it says "please, I need money now." Your heart drops before your mind can think. That is exactly what the caller wants. This post gives you a few simple habits that protect you even when the voice sounds perfect.

The short answer

You cannot tell a real voice from a copied one by listening alone, so do not try. Check by another route. Hang up, then call the person back on a number you already have. Do not send money because of a voice or a video call alone.

  • Slow down. Real emergencies can survive five minutes of checking.
  • Hang up and call back on a saved number, not the number that called you.
  • Ask something only the real person could answer.
  • Call another relative or friend, even if the caller says "keep this secret."
  • Agree a family code word now, before anyone needs it.

How does a copied voice scam work?

The United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is a government body that protects shoppers. It warns that scammers can use artificial intelligence (AI) to copy the voice of someone you know. The FTC says a short audio clip, which may come from something posted online, plus a voice-copying program can be enough to make a call sound like your relative.

We will not explain how the programs work, and you do not need to know. What matters is the plan behind the call. A scammer wants you to feel fear and to act before you think.

The caller may say they are your child, a cousin, a friend, or even a lawyer, a police officer or a doctor. The story is always urgent: an accident, an arrest, a hospital bill, a fee at school. You are told you are the only one who can help. You are asked to tell nobody.

This is an old trick with a new tool. Tanzania's communications regulator, the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority (TCRA), has long told people to be careful with messages such as "your son is sick at school" and not to cooperate with them. A copied voice only makes the same story feel more real.

Why this matters in East Africa

In August 2026, INTERPOL published its African Cyberthreat Assessment Report. INTERPOL says artificial intelligence is enabling 55 per cent of the cybercrimes reported across Africa. It also says AI-made fake media, often called deepfakes, often support sextortion and online harassment. The report names East Africa as a hub for mobile money fraud.

We want to be careful here. That report does not say how many cases in Tanzania involve a copied voice, and we did not find a verified local case to describe, so we will not invent one. What it does show is that criminals are using these tools and that mobile money is a target. If you use M-Pesa, Tigo Pesa or Airtel Money, the habits below are for you.

Signs that a call or video is a trap

Your ears and eyes are not a reliable test. Look at what the caller asks for and how they ask. The FTC lists these warning signs, and they match what TCRA tells the public.

What you hear or seeWhat it may meanWhat to do
"Send money now, there is no time"They want to stop you thinkingSay you will call back and hang up
"Do not tell anyone"They fear you will checkCall another relative anyway
An unknown number, or a new number "because my phone broke"The real person is not callingCall the saved number
A request to send by mobile money to a number you do not knowMoney that is hard to get backDo not send. Ask for a call on video with a person you can name
A person claiming to be police, a lawyer or a doctorA false authorityContact the real office yourself
Crying, shouting, a poor lineNoise hides small errorsDo not rely on the sound at all

A video call is not proof either. Fake video exists too. Do not trust lip movement, blinking or picture quality as a test. Nobody can promise that such signs show up, and tools that claim to "detect" fakes are not something you should depend on. Use your own checks instead.

Five checks that work even when the voice sounds real

These checks do not depend on spotting a fake. They work because the scammer cannot easily pass them.

  1. Pause and hang up. Say "I will call you right back" and end the call. A real person in real trouble will understand. A scammer will push you to stay on the line.
  2. Call back on a number you already know. Use the contact saved in your phone, or call another number you trust, such as a school office or an employer's main line. Do not press "call back" on the missed call and do not use a number the caller gives you.
  3. Ask something only the real person knows. Choose a question that cannot be found online: the name of a childhood pet, what you ate last time you met. Do not ask something that is on their social media.
  4. Use a family code word. This is our suggestion, not an official rule. Agree one word or short phrase with the people close to you, and say it only in a real emergency. Pick something people cannot guess, and do not post it or send it in a group chat. If a caller cannot say it, stop.
  5. Contact someone else. Phone another relative, a friend or a neighbour who might know where the person is. The FTC advises this even when you were told to keep the matter secret.

If the call claims to be from your boss or a business partner, add one more rule to the list: no payment is made on a voice or a message alone. Send money only through the normal approval your workplace already uses, and confirm any change of account number in person or by calling a number you already hold.

Say you are the manager of a small shop in Mwanza. A voice that sounds like your supplier asks you to send TSh 800,000 to a new number "because the old one is blocked." That is an example, not a real case. The safe answer is: "I will call you back on the number I have." Then you call the number saved in your phone. If the supplier knows nothing about it, you have saved TSh 800,000.

What if the caller threatens or begs?

Stay kind to yourself. Panic is normal. The scam is designed to cause it. You do not need to argue, explain or be polite for long. You can say "I will call you back" and put the phone down.

If you are afraid for someone, turn that fear into action that is safe. Ring the person on the saved number. Ring the school, the hospital or the police station yourself, using a number you find on your own. If the real person answers and is fine, you can relax. If they cannot be reached, ask another relative to help you look for them before any money moves.

What can you do before anyone calls?

A little preparation makes you harder to trick.

  • Talk to older relatives. Parents and grandparents are often the target. Show them this page and practise the words "I will call you back."
  • Choose your family code word.
  • Think about what you post. Short clips of your voice on public pages can be copied. You do not have to stop sharing, but you can set accounts to friends only if that suits you.
  • Save the numbers of close relatives, your children's school and your bank or mobile money agent in your phone.
  • Ask your mobile money provider what protections it offers for your account, and use them.

If you already sent money

Act quickly. The sooner you report, the better the chance of help.

  1. Contact your mobile money provider or bank straight away and tell them what happened. TCRA suggests dialling 100 to reach your service provider.
  2. Report to the police. TCRA's frequently asked questions page says fraud is a police matter: go to a police station to report it and get an RB number (a police report number).
  3. Report the scammer's number to TCRA by SMS to 15040. TCRA pages describe the text slightly differently, so follow the automatic reply you receive. It will tell you what to send. You can also call TCRA free on 0800008272 for more information.
  4. Tell your family, so nobody else is caught by the same number.
  5. Keep screenshots, call logs and payment messages. Do not delete them.

We cannot promise that money will come back. Being quick helps, and so does having clear records.

If someone uses a fake video or voice to threaten you or share private pictures, do not pay and do not reply. Keep the evidence and report it to the police. It is not your fault.

Common questions

Can I tell a fake voice by listening carefully?

No, not reliably. Do not depend on your ear. The checks above work even when the voice is perfect.

Is a video call proof that the person is real?

No. Fake video exists, and you should not trust small visual signs. Use the same checks: call back on a saved number, ask a private question and never send money on a call alone.

Should I use an AI detection tool?

We cannot say that any such tool is dependable, and we did not find an official recommendation for one. Rely on your own habits instead.

What if the person really is in trouble?

Then checking will take only a few minutes, and the real person will not mind. Call them, call someone near them, and help in a way you can confirm, such as paying a hospital directly after you speak to the hospital on a number you found yourself.

Where do I report a scam call in Tanzania?

Go to a police station for an RB number. You can also report the number to TCRA by SMS to 15040 and follow the automatic reply. Details can change, so check the TCRA website for the current wording.

What to do next

  1. Choose a family code word today and tell the people you love.
  2. Save key numbers in your phone and teach one older relative to say "I will call you back."
  3. Read more about common job-offer scams in Tanzania, which use the same pressure tricks.
  4. Before you use any chatbot, learn how to write a good AI prompt and how AI chatbots work in plain words.

A scammer borrows a voice, but they cannot borrow your habits. A calm pause protects the people you love, and you can learn it in five minutes.

Sources and further reading

  • Scammers use fake emergencies to steal your money, Federal Trade Commission
  • INTERPOL report finds AI linked to more than half of cybercrime in Africa, INTERPOL
  • Frequently asked questions on customer and consumer affairs, TCRA
  • TCRA launches campaign to curb online fraud, TCRA

Reporting details were read on the TCRA pages in November 2026. They may change, so check the TCRA website before you report.

item.title: Ajira Portal: How to Apply for Public Service Jobs Step by Step
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: What to prepare, how the Ajira Portal works and which mistakes get a government job application rejected. Plain steps for first-time applicants.
item.content:encoded:
Waiting for a government job can feel heavy, especially when you have done everything right and still hear nothing. A clean application is the part you control. This post shows how applying through the Ajira Portal works, what to prepare first and which small mistakes cost people their chance.

The short answer

For jobs advertised by the Public Service Recruitment Secretariat (PSRS), you apply online through the Ajira recruitment portal. Prepare your certified documents before you start, create your account with an email address you can open, fill your profile honestly, and send the application for the post you want.

  • Apply only through the official portal. The advert we read says applications sent by any other means will not be considered.
  • Read the advert for the post. Each advert has its own conditions, qualifications and deadline.
  • Scan certified copies of your certificates. Do not scan Form IV or Form VI result slips if the advert says they are not accepted.
  • Name three referees with contacts that work.
  • Never pay anyone to apply for you or to "push" your application.

What the Public Service Recruitment Secretariat does

The PSRS is part of the President's Office. When public institutions need staff, the PSRS publishes a vacancy announcement on their behalf. The announcement we read in November 2026 was written for the Tanzania Electric Supply Company (TANESCO), and it said the PSRS was inviting applications on behalf of that company.

This matters because the advert is your rulebook. It lists the duties of each post, the qualifications and the general conditions for all applicants. You apply on the strength of what the advert says.

The government main portal also lists other official systems for jobs. Besides the PSRS portal, it names a portal for health cadre jobs run through the Ministry of Health and another for teaching and health jobs run through TAMISEMI. Check which one your advert points to. This post is about the PSRS portal, but the habits in it help on all of them.

We could not open the portal's own applicant guide when we checked in November 2026. The portal pages did not show their content to our tools. So we do not describe each screen here. Screens and buttons can change, and the portal's own guide is the best source for the exact layout.

Documents to prepare before you open the portal

Do this part first. Hunting for a document while the page is open is how people make mistakes.

The general conditions in the October 2026 advert asked applicants to attach certified copies of these items:

  • Degree, diploma or certificate (whatever the post asks for)
  • Transcripts for degrees and diplomas
  • Professional registration and training certificates, where the post needs them
  • Birth certificate

The same advert said it would not accept Form IV and Form VI result slips, testimonials or partial transcripts. Other conditions in that advert included:

  • A recent passport-size photo uploaded to the portal
  • Three reputable referees with contacts that work
  • Foreign certificates recognised by the right authorities (TCU, NECTA and NACTVET were named)
  • A signed application letter in Swahili or English

These are the conditions of one advert. Another advert may add or change rules, for example on age limits. Always read the conditions section of the advert you are answering, then work from that list.

The Ministry of Health portal guide gives a similar list for health jobs. It also asks for a CV, a passport photo, a NIDA number if you have one, and an application letter. If your names differ across documents, it asks for proof of a change of name. This is guidance for that portal only, but it shows a good habit: make sure your name is spelled the same on every document.

Put everything in one folder on your phone or computer. Name each file clearly, for example degree-certificate.pdf. Check each scan is readable before you upload it.

How to create your account and fill your profile

Here is what the Ministry of Health guide describes for its own portal. We read it in November 2026. It is not a guide to the PSRS portal, so expect differences.

  1. Use a valid email address that you can open. The account name is your email and you choose a password.
  2. Choose the right category when asked. The guide warns that a wrong choice can stop you from going further.
  3. Fill in personal details such as your names, date of birth, phone number and email.
  4. Add your academic qualifications, then professional qualifications if you have them.
  5. Add working experience and language skills.
  6. Attach your documents and send the application.

Take your time on the profile. Many portals keep your profile for later applications, so careful work now saves time in the future. Write your names exactly as they appear on your certificates.

Keep your password somewhere safe, and do not share it. If a stranger offers to "create your account," you are giving them access to your personal documents, your NIDA details and your future applications.

How to apply for one vacancy

Once your profile is ready, the steps are simple in idea, even if the screens differ:

  1. Find the advert for the post you want on the official PSRS page or the portal. Read the duties, the qualifications and the general conditions.
  2. Check honestly that you meet the qualifications. If the advert asks for a certain level of study or registration and you do not have it, wait for a post that fits.
  3. Prepare your signed application letter. Our post on how to write an application letter shows a simple layout.
  4. Write a CV that matches the advert. See how to write a CV for your first job.
  5. Choose the post in the portal, attach the right documents and review everything.
  6. Send the application before the deadline in the advert. Do not wait for the last day, so a slow connection does not cost you the chance.

The October 2026 advert said the letter should be addressed to the Secretary of the PSRS at an address in Dodoma. Because adverts can change, copy the address from the advert you are using and not from this page.

After you send it, keep a copy of what you submitted. The advert we read said only shortlisted candidates are told the date of an interview. So no news does not always mean you were rejected, but it does mean you should keep checking the official page.

Mistakes that get applications rejected

  • Applying by another route. The advert said anything sent outside the portal will not be considered. Emailing or delivering a bundle of papers is not enough.
  • Uncertified copies. The advert asked for certified copies. Ask the right office to certify your copies early, because it can take a few days.
  • Sending slips the advert refuses. Form IV and Form VI result slips and testimonials were listed as not accepted in that advert.
  • Weak referees. Choose three people who know your work, tell them first, and check their phone numbers and emails.
  • Wrong or mixed names. If your birth certificate and your degree show different names, find out how to prove they are the same person before you apply.
  • False information. The advert warned that forged certificates and false information lead to legal action. Never take that risk. A real, modest record is better than a fake one.
  • Paying a "helper". The portal route does not need a middleman. Read our post on fake job offers before you pay anyone anything.

Common questions

Can I apply for a government job by email or by hand?

For PSRS adverts, the one we read said all applications must be sent through the recruitment portal and anything else will not be considered. Check each advert.

Do I need to pay to use the Ajira Portal?

The advert did not mention any fee for applying. Be careful with anyone who asks for money for jobs, shortlisting or interviews. If you are unsure, ask the official office named in the advert.

Can I use one account for several vacancies?

Portals normally keep your profile for later use, but we could not confirm how the PSRS portal handles this. Check the portal's guide.

What if I am already working in the public service?

The October 2026 advert said public servants should follow a government circular and not apply directly, and that retired public servants should not apply. Other adverts may differ, so read the conditions.

What to do next

  1. Gather your certificates and ask for certified copies now, before any advert comes.
  2. Choose three referees, ask each one, and write down their contacts.
  3. Make a clear CV and a draft application letter that you can adjust for each post.
  4. When a post fits you, open the official advert, read every condition and apply through the portal well before the deadline.

Applying well is a skill, and you get better each time. Keep going, and be proud that you are doing it honestly.

Sources and further reading

  • Vacancy announcement for TANESCO posts, 13 October 2026, Public Service Recruitment Secretariat
  • Ministry of Health Ajira Portal user guide, Ministry of Health
  • Kazi, Ajira na Mahusiano (jobs and labour topics), Government of Tanzania

item.title: Apollo 11: How People First Landed on the Moon in 1969
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: What happened on Apollo 11, from launch on 16 July 1969 to splashdown on 24 July: the crew, the landing, the moonwalk, what they left, and common myths.
item.content:encoded:
In July 1969, three men flew to the Moon, and two of them walked on it. Hundreds of millions of people watched on television. If you have ever looked up at the Moon and wondered how it was done, this post tells the story in plain words, using NASA and the Smithsonian as our main sources.

The short answer

Apollo 11 was the first mission to land people on the Moon. It lifted off on 16 July 1969, the lunar module Eagle landed on 20 July, and the crew splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on 24 July 1969.

  • The crew was Neil Armstrong (commander), Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin (lunar module pilot) and Michael Collins (command module pilot).
  • Armstrong and Aldrin landed in the Sea of Tranquility. Collins stayed in orbit.
  • They spent 21 hours and 36 minutes on the surface, and the moonwalk itself lasted a little over two and a half hours.
  • They left a plaque and other items behind and brought back 47 pounds (21.5 kilograms) of Moon rock and soil.

Why did the United States try to reach the Moon?

The Moon race grew out of the Cold War, the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union. The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum says the Soviet Union sent the first person into space, Yuri Gagarin, on 12 April 1961. Days later, President John F. Kennedy asked Vice President Lyndon Johnson to find a space programme the United States could win. On 25 May 1961, Kennedy told Congress that the country should aim to explore the Moon with people.

It took eight years and a huge rocket to do it. NASA lists the launch vehicle as a Saturn V.

Who were the crew?

  • Neil Armstrong, commander. He was the first person to walk on the Moon.
  • Buzz Aldrin, lunar module pilot. He walked on the Moon after Armstrong.
  • Michael Collins, command module pilot. He flew the spacecraft Columbia and stayed in orbit around the Moon while the others went down.

Collins's role is often forgotten, yet the mission needed him in orbit. NASA names three backup astronauts: James Lovell, Fred Haise and William Anders.

What happened from launch to landing?

The mission ran for eight days. Here are the main steps, based on NASA's mission overview.

  1. 16 July 1969. The Saturn V rocket lifted off from Launch Pad 39A in Florida at 9:32 a.m. Eastern time.
  2. Journey to the Moon. The crew travelled in Columbia, joined to the lunar module Eagle.
  3. 20 July. Armstrong and Aldrin flew Eagle down to the Moon. It landed in the Sea of Tranquility, about four miles from the planned spot and about a minute and a half early, says NASA. The Smithsonian gives the distance as about 6 kilometres, which is the same distance in different units.
  4. Manual flying. The Smithsonian says Armstrong flew the last minutes by hand to avoid a crater about 180 metres wide.
  5. First steps. Armstrong stepped onto the surface about 109 hours and 42 minutes after launch. Aldrin followed about 20 minutes later.

NASA prints Armstrong's first words from the surface as "...one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind." Some people discuss whether he said "a man" or just "man". We use NASA's wording and leave that debate aside.

The Smithsonian estimates that about 650 million people watched around the world. It is an estimate, as nobody counted exactly.

What did they do on the Moon?

Be careful with two different times, because they are often mixed up.

  • Time on the surface: 21 hours and 36 minutes. This is how long Eagle stayed on the Moon.
  • Moonwalk: more than two and a half hours. This is the time the two men spent outside.

During the moonwalk, Aldrin set up the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package. The men also collected samples, and both walked up to about 300 feet from Eagle. NASA says Aldrin was outside for 1 hour and 33 minutes before going back in, and Armstrong followed 41 minutes later.

After the walk, they rested and then took off to meet Collins in orbit. The three flew home. The command module splashed down on 24 July 1969 at 12:50 p.m. Eastern time, about 13 miles from the recovery ship USS Hornet. NASA says the landing point was moved about 250 miles because of weather. The whole flight lasted 195 hours, 18 minutes and 35 seconds.

What did they leave, and what came back?

Left on the Moon, according to NASA:

  • A plaque on the lunar module's descent stage. NASA's mission page says it was signed by President Richard Nixon and the three astronauts. Its words are: "Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind."
  • Medallions honouring the three Apollo 1 astronauts and two Soviet cosmonauts who died in accidents.
  • A small silicon disk, 1.5 inches wide, with goodwill messages from leaders of 73 countries.

Also left was a laser reflector, an array of 100 small mirrors in a 10 by 10 grid, put down on 21 July 1969, according to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. It sends light straight back to where it came from.

Brought back: 47 pounds (21.5 kilograms) of lunar rock and soil, says NASA. Other NASA and Smithsonian pages give slightly different weights, such as 21.7 or 21.8 kilograms, because of how samples are counted. All are close to the same amount.

Myths and facts about the landing

Some people say the landing was staged. We do not list every claim, but one fact is easy to check. The laser reflector Apollo 11 left is still used. The JPL says observatories such as McDonald Observatory in Texas and one near Grasse in France fire lasers at it. NASA's 2020 article says research with these Apollo-era reflectors continues. People in many countries can measure the returning light, so this evidence does not rest on NASA alone.

We do not credit Apollo with inventing everyday products, because we found no NASA page that says so.

Why does Apollo 11 still inspire students?

The mission shows what many people can do when they work together on a hard problem. The three astronauts were the most visible people, but a mission like this needs many kinds of skill on the ground as well as in space.

You do not need a rocket to start. Maths, physics and careful reading are the first steps. If you are a student in Tanzania who likes science, the same subjects open many doors, from engineering to data work. We cannot promise any particular career, and you should check what each course requires. Yet the habit of asking a big question and working on it step by step is open to everyone.

Common questions

Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?

Neil Armstrong. Buzz Aldrin followed about 20 minutes later, according to NASA.

How long did Apollo 11 take?

From launch on 16 July to splashdown on 24 July 1969. NASA gives the total flight time as 195 hours, 18 minutes and 35 seconds.

Did anyone stay in the lunar module the whole time?

No. Armstrong and Aldrin went down in Eagle while Collins stayed in orbit in Columbia.

How many people watched?

An estimated 650 million, according to NASA and the Smithsonian. It is an estimate.

What to do next

  1. Read NASA's mission overview and compare it with the Smithsonian story below.
  2. Find the Sea of Tranquility on a Moon map or in an astronomy app.
  3. Practise one subject you need for science, such as maths or physics, a little each day.

A small step done again and again can take you a long way.

Sources and further reading

  • Apollo 11 Mission Overview, NASA
  • Apollo 11 Plaque, NASA Science
  • Apollo 11 Moon Landing, National Air and Space Museum
  • Apollo 11 Experiment Still Going Strong after 35 Years, NASA JPL
  • Retroreflectors: From Apollo to Mars, NASA
  • Space Samples Link NASA's Apollo 11 and Mars 2020, NASA

item.title: Back Up Your Files: Free Cloud Storage and the 3-2-1 Rule
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: How to keep school and family files safe with the 3-2-1 rule, free Google and OneDrive storage, Windows Backup and a second copy on a drive.
item.content:encoded:
Few feelings are worse than a laptop that will not turn on the week before a deadline. Your final-year project is inside it. So are the photos of people you love. A back-up is how you make sure that one broken machine is a bad day and not a disaster.

This post is about files on a computer: school work, documents and photos. It is not about phones. For phones, read how to back up your phone and move to a new one.

The short answer

Keep three copies of every file that matters, on two kinds of storage, with one copy away from home. A simple version is the original on your laptop, a copy on an external drive, and a copy in free cloud storage. Then check once in a while that you can open the copy.

  • Your laptop is copy one.
  • An external hard drive or flash disk is copy two.
  • Cloud storage, such as Google or OneDrive, is copy three and it is away from your room.
  • Set it to run by itself when you can, because people forget.
  • Test a restore: open a file from the back-up and check it works.

What is the 3-2-1 rule?

The US cyber agency CISA recommends this rule. It says to keep three copies of important files, to store them on two different types of storage (for example a hard drive and the cloud), and to keep one copy off-site, away from where you work.

Why three? One copy can break, and so can a second. Why two types? A hard drive can fail in a way a cloud account does not, and the other way round. Why one away from home? Fire, flood and theft hit the whole room at once. The cloud counts as off-site.

CISA also says a back-up that runs on its own, on a regular schedule, protects against hardware failure and damage. It also says you should practise restoring, so that you know it works before the day you need it.

How much free cloud storage is there?

Free storage is a good third copy for school work and key photos. Here is what the providers say. As checked in November 2026, these figures can change, so read the live pages before you rely on them.

ProviderFree amountGood to know
Google accountup to 15 GBShared by Gmail, Drive and Google Photos
Microsoft account (OneDrive)5 GBNeeds a free Microsoft account

Google says the 15 GB is shared. Your emails count, including those in Spam and Trash, and so do files in Drive and photos in Google Photos. If you go over the limit, you can still sign in, but you cannot upload new files to Drive or back up photos to Google Photos. Gmail may also stop sending and receiving. Google also says content may be removed if an account stays over the limit for two years or more, and it says it will warn you well before that.

So keep an eye on the number. Delete big files you do not need, and keep documents (small) separate from videos (big).

15 GB is room for many documents and a good number of photos, but not for hours of video. If your work is big, tell yourself which files matter most and back those up first: school work, ID scans, family photos.

How do I back up with Windows Backup and OneDrive?

Microsoft's Windows Backup app is included in Windows 10 and Windows 11. You can find it by searching "backup" in the Start menu. It can back up files and settings. With OneDrive folder back-up you turn on your Desktop, Documents, Pictures, Videos or Music folders, and they are copied to your OneDrive. You can then open them on any PC where you sign in with the same account.

Some things to know, from Microsoft's page:

  • It needs a personal Microsoft account (for example an outlook.com address). Work or school accounts will not work.
  • A free Microsoft account has 5 GB of OneDrive storage. You can buy more, but you do not have to.
  • To check the status, go to Settings, then Accounts, then Windows backup.
  • To restore, sign in with the same account on a new PC or after you reinstall Windows, and choose to restore. You can also sign in to OneDrive to get your files.

Microsoft says Windows 10 support ended on 14 October 2025, with no more free updates or security fixes. If your laptop still runs Windows 10, back up first, and then read Microsoft's page about moving to Windows 11. Our guide on speeding up a slow Windows PC may also help an older machine.

If you do not use Windows, or do not want to put your files into OneDrive, simply copy your important folders into Google Drive in your browser. The idea is the same.

How do I keep a second copy on a drive?

A drive gives you a copy that does not need the internet. This matters when data is expensive or the network is down. CISA also says to make sure your critical files can be reached without internet.

Here is a plain method that needs no special tool:

  1. Plug in your external hard drive or a large flash disk.
  2. Make a folder on it named "Backup" and the date, for example "Backup 2026-11".
  3. Copy your important folders into it by dragging them in File Explorer.
  4. Wait until the copy finishes, then eject the drive safely.
  5. Keep the drive somewhere safe, not in the same bag as the laptop.

We did not open Microsoft's steps for File History, so we do not describe it here. Copying by hand works fine if you do it on a regular day, such as the first Sunday of every month.

Flash disks are small and easy to lose, and they can get a virus from other computers. Do not make one flash disk your only copy. We do not recommend any paid back-up product here, and you do not need one to follow this plan.

How do I know my back-up works?

A back-up you have never opened is only a hope. Once a month, do a quick test.

  • Open the Backup folder or your cloud account.
  • Pick one file and open it. Check that it is the latest version.
  • Look at the date of the newest file. If it is old, something has stopped.

Say you save your project in a folder called "Project". If the copy in the cloud shows last month's file, you have found the problem while it is still small.

Common questions

Is a flash disk a back-up?

It can be one copy, but not your only one. Flash disks break, get lost and carry viruses. Use it with a cloud copy.

Is the cloud safe?

Cloud services keep your files away from your room, which helps against loss. You still need a strong password on the account. Choose a long password that you use nowhere else, and keep the recovery details for the account up to date.

What if I run out of free space?

Delete what you no longer need, or choose which files matter most. You can buy more space, but you do not have to. Never pay a stranger who offers "storage".

How often should I back up?

Back up whenever you finish something you cannot make again. For school work, that can be every time you finish a session. For other files, once a month is a good habit.

What to do next

  1. Today, copy your most important folder to a flash disk or hard drive.
  2. Sign in to Google Drive or OneDrive and upload that same folder, or turn on OneDrive folder back-up.
  3. Set a reminder on your phone for the first day of every month to check the copy.
  4. Check the live pages of Google and Microsoft for the current free storage.

You are protecting the work you have done and the memories you care about. That is worth one hour of your time.

Sources and further reading

  • Back up business data, CISA
  • How storage works in your Google Account, Google Account Help
  • Back up your Windows PC, Microsoft Support
  • Free Office online for the web, Microsoft

item.title: Back Up Your Phone and Move to a New One Without Losing Data
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Back up your photos, contacts and chats first, then move them to a new phone with Google, Apple Quick Start or Move to iOS. See what does not move too.
item.content:encoded:
On your phone are the faces of the people you love, and the messages you may want to read again. Losing them hurts more than losing the phone. A new phone should never mean a fresh start you did not choose.

This post helps you save what matters first, then move it across with three clear paths.

The short answer

Back up your old phone to your account, sign in on the new phone, and restore during setup. Keep both phones charged and on Wi-Fi. Do not erase or sell the old phone until you have checked that your photos, contacts and chats are on the new one.

  • Back up first, even if you think you are safe.
  • Check that you have enough free storage in your account and on the new phone.
  • Use Wi-Fi, not mobile data, because backups can be large.
  • Some things do not move. Check them one by one.
  • Moving a SIM card or mobile-money line is a separate matter for your operator.

Before you do anything: back up and check your storage

  1. Charge the old phone, and connect it to Wi-Fi.
  2. Write down your account details: your Google Account or Apple Account and its password. You will need them on the new phone.
  3. Check your storage. A backup needs space in your account, and the new phone needs room for everything you move. Google says an account has 15 GB of free backup storage, with more available if you pay (Google Android Help, as checked in November 2026).
  4. Back up your WhatsApp chats separately (see below).
  5. Keep the old phone until you finish.

If your storage is almost full, our post on how much RAM and storage you need explains how to see what uses the space.

Android to Android: Google backup and restore

Google says Android can back up apps and app data, call history, contacts, device settings and SMS and MMS messages. Photos and videos are kept by Google Photos if you use it (Google Android Help, as checked in November 2026).

To back up now, open Settings, tap Google, then All services. Under Backup and restore, tap Backup, then Back up now. Menu names may differ by brand and Android version.

To restore, turn on the new phone and follow the setup screens. When you add your Google Account, you can choose the earlier backup. Google says the process can take up to 24 hours to complete fully, so be patient.

Two limits to know:

  • A backup made on a newer Android cannot be restored onto a phone that runs a lower Android. If the new phone is behind the old one, the transfer may be incomplete.
  • Contacts saved only on the SIM card may need to be restored by hand. Google links to a separate guide for this.

iPhone to iPhone, and Android to iPhone

iPhone to iPhone with Quick Start

Apple says the other phone must be an iPhone or iPad with iOS 11 or iPadOS 13 or later, and both should be updated. Put the new phone near the old one. The old phone must be unlocked, on the Home Screen, on Wi-Fi with Bluetooth on. Follow the prompts, then choose a transfer method.

There are two main ways. With iCloud download, apps and data come down in the background and you can start using the new phone right away. With direct transfer, you must wait until the transfer finishes on both phones. Keep both phones near each other and plugged in until it is done (Apple Support, as checked in November 2026).

Android to iPhone with Move to iOS

Apple says the iPhone must be new or erased. On the new iPhone, choose to set up without another Apple device, then choose to transfer from Android. On the Android phone, open the Move to iOS app and enter the code the iPhone shows. Keep both phones plugged in and close to each other until the loading bar ends, and do not use other apps on the Android phone meanwhile.

Apple lists what can move: contacts, messages, camera photos and videos, files, bookmarks, mail accounts, WhatsApp messages and media, call history and calendars. Some free apps move if they exist on both stores. All of it must fit on the iPhone (Apple Support, as checked in November 2026). Newer versions may also offer a method without the app. Read Apple's page for the current steps.

WhatsApp: back it up on its own

WhatsApp's help page says that on Android you open WhatsApp, tap Settings, then Chats, then Chat backup, and tap Back up. Connect to Wi-Fi first, because backup files can be large and may use mobile data. You can also turn on an end-to-end encrypted backup. If you do, keep the password or key safe, because without it you cannot open the backup later (WhatsApp Help Center, as checked in November 2026).

For the restore itself, we did not confirm the details. Follow the WhatsApp restore screen on the new phone and read WhatsApp's own help page.

What does not move, and how to check

Do not promise yourself that everything will move. Plan to check.

  • Music, books and PDFs do not move from Android to iPhone with Move to iOS. Copy them yourself.
  • Most apps need to be installed again, and some need you to sign in again.
  • SIM-only contacts may need to be restored by hand on Android.
  • Chats in other apps may not move. Look inside each app for its own backup option.
  • Your phone number and mobile-money line are tied to your SIM and your operator. We did not find a source to describe the steps, so ask your operator.

After the move, spend ten minutes checking:

  1. Open your photos and scroll to the oldest ones.
  2. Open your contacts and compare the count with the old phone.
  3. Open your most important chats.
  4. Open the apps you use daily and sign in.
  5. Check your files and downloads.

Only when all of this looks right should you erase the old phone. Keep it a few more days if you can.

Common questions

How long does it take?

It depends on how much you have and on your network. Google says a restore can take up to 24 hours to complete fully. Apple says transfer time depends on the network and the amount of data.

Will mobile data be used?

Backups can be large. Use Wi-Fi where you can, as WhatsApp itself advises.

What if my backup account is full?

Free up space, buy more storage, or move your photos to a computer. Do not delete anything until you have a copy.

Can I move from iPhone to Android?

We did not check a source for this path, so we do not cover it here. Look at the maker's official pages.

What to do next

  1. Back up your phone today, before anything goes wrong.
  2. Write down your account passwords somewhere safe.
  3. When you get the new phone, choose the path above that fits and keep both phones plugged in.
  4. Check your photos, contacts and chats before you erase the old phone.

Your memories are worth ten careful minutes. Take them slowly and they will be waiting for you on the new phone.

Sources and further reading

  • Back up or restore data on your Android device, Google Android Help
  • Use Quick Start to transfer data to a new iPhone, Apple Support
  • Move from Android to iPhone or iPad, Apple Support
  • How to back up your chat history, WhatsApp Help Center

item.title: Branding Basics: Name, Logo and Colours for a Small Business
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: How to choose a simple business name, two colours, one font and a plain logo, and use them the same way on your sign, phone, receipts and social pages.
item.content:encoded:
Every small business starts as an idea in one person's head. A brand is how that idea becomes something other people recognise and remember. You do not need an agency or a big budget to start. You need a few clear choices, made once and kept.

The short answer

A brand is what customers think of when they think of your business. Your name, logo, colours and fonts are the part people can see. Keep them simple and use them the same way everywhere.

  • Pick a name that is easy to say, spell and search for.
  • Choose two colours and one font, and stick with them.
  • Keep the logo plain enough to read on a small phone screen and on a signboard.
  • Use the same look on your sign, receipts, social pages and Google listing.
  • Registering a business name with BRELA is a separate task from design.

What is a brand, really?

The Queensland Government's small business guide describes a brand as what customers and potential customers think of when they think of your business. It includes things you can touch, like your shop, and things you cannot, like your reputation and service. It calls brand identity the part people can see, hear and experience: the business name, logo, tagline, colours, fonts, graphics and images.

So a logo alone is not a brand. If your logo looks smart but you reply slowly and give the wrong change, people remember that. The same guide says what your brand says and does should be the same.

That is good news. You can start building a brand today, because the biggest part is how you treat customers.

How do I choose a business name?

The Queensland guide suggests a name or logo should be simple, memorable, ownable (clearly yours), enduring and versatile. Here is how to turn that into a test you can do in an afternoon.

  1. Say it. Say the name out loud to three people. Can they repeat it?
  2. Spell it. Ask them to write it. If they get it wrong, it may be too hard.
  3. Search it. Type it into Google, Instagram and Facebook. Is there a business with a very similar name doing something similar? If so, people may mix you up. Choose another.
  4. Check it will still fit. If you may add products later, avoid a name that boxes you in, like "Mama Neema Bicycle Spare Parts" if you may sell motorcycle parts next year.
  5. Think of both languages. In Tanzania, many customers use Kiswahili and English. Check the name does not sound odd or rude in either.
  6. Keep it short. Short names fit on signboards, receipts and phone screens.

Do not copy a famous name or a name that is very close to one. It can confuse customers, and it can cause legal trouble. For questions about trademarks and intellectual property, the Queensland guide says to always seek legal advice.

How do I pick colours, a font and a logo?

Choose few things and repeat them.

Two colours
