Pick one main colour and one second colour. Add white or black for text and background. Look at them on a phone screen in daylight. Is the text easy to read on the background? If you have to squint, change it.

Colours are your choice, not a rule. A paint shop, a cloth seller and a pharmacy may all want different feelings. Pick what suits you and your customers, and do not copy another business's colours.

One font

Use one clear font for your name and text. A plain, easy-to-read font is better than a fancy one that people cannot read from across the road. Check the font's licence if you plan to use it on a printed sign.

A simple logo

A good small-business logo can be your name in your chosen font and colour, with one simple shape if you like. Test it:

  • Does it look fine very small, like on a WhatsApp profile picture?
  • Does it still work in one colour, for example on a stamp or a receipt?
  • Is it your own work, not a copy or an edited version of someone else's logo?

Only use pictures and symbols you have the right to use. If a freelance designer makes it, agree in writing who owns the finished design.

How do I use the same look everywhere?

This is where small businesses can beat bigger ones. The Queensland guide says to apply your brand rules to every place customers meet you: website, social media, brochures, vehicles, uniforms. It also suggests writing the rules down in a style guide.

Yours can fit on one page:

  • Business name, written exactly one way.
  • Two colours, with their codes if you use a phone design app.
  • One font.
  • Where the logo goes on a sign, a receipt and a social media profile.
  • How you greet customers, in one sentence.

Then check each place:

  • Signboard or stall: same name and colours.
  • WhatsApp Business or social pages: same profile picture, same name.
  • Receipts and notebooks: name and phone number at the top.
  • Bags, boxes or uniforms: a small logo or name.
  • Phone number: the same one everywhere.

What name should I use on Google?

If your business appears on Google Maps, the name matters. Google's Business Profile help says your name should reflect your business's real-world name, as it appears on your storefront, website and stationery and as customers know it. It says not to add extra information, such as keywords, hours or taglines.

So if your sign says "Neema Fashions", use "Neema Fashions" on Google, not "Neema Fashions Best Cheap Tailor Mwanza Open 8am". Unneeded additions can cause problems with the listing. This is why a simple, steady name helps: you set it once.

Is registering a name with BRELA part of branding?

No. Branding is how you look and sound to customers. Registration is a legal step. They are different jobs.

As checked in November 2026, the BRELA page on registering business names says (the page is in Kiswahili):

  • One person, or a group of up to 20 people, may register a business name.
  • The applicant must be Tanzanian and at least 18 years old.
  • The steps are done online in BRELA's registration system.
  • Payment is by mobile money or bank, and the application is processed after payment is received.

The page lists no fees and has no separate name-check step, so we cannot tell you the cost. BRELA lists trade and service mark registration as a separate service from business name registration. We could not read the trade mark page, so we do not explain it here. Ask BRELA for the current steps, fees and what each registration protects. Check brela.go.tz.

Common questions

Do I need a professional logo designer?

Not to begin. A clear name in a clear font and two colours can do the job. A designer can help later if your business grows. Agree on ownership first.

Can I change my name or colours later?

You can, but people need time to learn it. Change rarely, and tell customers when you do.

Should my name include what I sell?

It can help people understand you, but it can also limit you later. Choose based on your plans for the next few years.

Is a brand the same as a trademark?

No. A brand is how customers know you. A trade mark is a legal registration. BRELA treats it as a separate service. Ask BRELA or a lawyer.

What to do next

  1. Write your business name on paper and run the say, spell and search test with three people.
  2. Pick two colours and one font. Write them on one page.
  3. Check that your sign, WhatsApp, social page and Google listing all show the same name.
  4. Visit brela.go.tz or ask BRELA about registering your business name, and ask what each step costs.

Great businesses are often remembered for small, steady things done the same way every day. Start with yours.

You can also read our posts on simple SEO for a small business website and on low-cost online business ideas in Tanzania.

Sources and further reading

  • Business branding, Business Queensland (Queensland Government)
  • Usajili wa Majina ya Biashara (business name registration), BRELA
  • Business Registrations and Licensing Agency, home page
  • Business name guidelines, Google Business Profile Help

item.title: Buying a Used Phone in Tanzania: What to Check Before You Pay
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: A calm, step-by-step check you can do at the counter before paying for a second-hand phone: IMEI, account locks, battery, screen, buttons and charging port.
item.content:encoded:
A used phone can save you a lot of money. It can also leave you with a phone that locks, dies by noon or never works properly. The seller usually knows more about the phone than you do, so you need a plan before you stand at the counter.

This post gives you a fixed order of checks. Do them every time, calmly, and be ready to walk away politely if something is wrong.

The short answer

Before you pay for a second-hand phone, check that it works, belongs to the seller and is free of any other person's account. Do not rush. A seller who is honest will not mind you taking ten minutes.

  • Get the IMEI (the phone's 15-digit ID number) and check it on the TCRA page. Make sure the details match the phone in your hand.
  • Make sure the previous owner's account is gone, so the phone does not lock on you later.
  • Test the screen, buttons, cameras, speaker, microphone and charging port.
  • Watch how the battery behaves while you test.
  • Ask for the seller's details and a receipt, and keep the box and charger if there are any.

Step 1: Get the IMEI and check it on the TCRA page

Every phone has an IMEI, a 15-digit number that identifies that one device. To see it, open the phone's dial pad and type *#06#. The number appears on the screen.

On an iPhone you can also find it in Settings, then General, then About. You may need to scroll down. Apple says iPhone 14 models and later have no IMEI engraving on the body, so older engraved numbers only apply to older models (Apple Support, as checked in November 2026).

The Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority (TCRA) has a public page for this. As checked in November 2026, the page says to dial *#06#, type the 15-digit number into the box and press Verify IMEI. The page then shows the model, the maker and the frequency bands. You compare these with the phone you are holding. The page also warns people to avoid fake devices.

Here is what that means for you:

  • If the model, maker or bands shown do not match the phone in your hand, do not buy it.
  • If the number on the screen is different from the number printed on the box or the tray, ask why. If the answer is not clear, do not buy it.

We could not find any statement on the TCRA page that it shows whether a phone is stolen or blocked. Do not treat a result as proof that a phone is clean. It is one check among several. A match tells you the phone is the model it claims to be. It does not tell you who owns it.

You can do the check on your own phone while standing at the counter. It takes about one minute and needs a little data.

Step 2: Make sure the phone is not locked to someone else

Modern phones are tied to the account of the person who set them up. If the seller does not remove that account, the phone can become useless in your hands. This is the single most important check, and many buyers skip it.

If it is an iPhone

Apple's advice for buyers is clear. Turn the phone on and unlock it. If you see a passcode lock screen or a home screen, the seller has not erased it yet. Ask them to erase it first.

Then start the setup. If the phone asks for the previous owner's Apple Account details, it is still linked to that person. Stop there. If you see an "iPhone Locked to Owner" screen, Apple says not to take ownership of it. The phone is ready for you only when the Hello screen appears (Apple Support, as checked in November 2026).

If the seller is not there, they would have to remove the phone from their account on the internet. That is a good reason to do this check in front of the seller.

If it is an Android phone

Google says that after a factory reset, an Android phone with this protection needs the Google Account that was added to it. If you cannot give that during setup, Google warns that you will not be able to use the device at all (Google Pixel Help, as checked in November 2026).

So the seller must remove their Google Account from the phone before you pay. Ask them to do it in front of you. The exact menu name may differ by brand and Android version, but it is usually found under Settings, in the accounts or passwords section.

After the seller has removed the account and reset the phone, turn it on and go through setup. If the phone asks you to sign in with an account you do not own, do not pay.

A short rule you can remember: the phone should reach a clean welcome screen and let you set it up as your own.

Step 3: Test the battery, screen, buttons, cameras and charging port

Once you know the phone is not locked, check that it works. Ask for a charger and a few minutes. Work through this list in order.

  1. Screen. Look at it in good light. Check for cracks, dark patches, coloured lines and dead spots. Drag your finger slowly across the whole screen, edge to edge, and see if it responds everywhere. A white screen helps show marks and a dark screen shows bright pixels.
  2. Buttons. Press volume up, volume down and the power button. Each should click and work every time.
  3. Cameras. Open the camera and test the back and front cameras. Take a photo and a short video. Zoom in on the photo and check that it is sharp and has no spots.
  4. Speaker and microphone. Play a song or video. Then record a voice note and play it back. Make a short phone call if you can.
  5. Charging port. Plug the cable in. It should sit firmly and the phone should show that it is charging. If you must wiggle the cable to make it charge, that is a warning sign.
  6. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and mobile network. Put in your own SIM card. Check that you get a signal and can open a web page.
  7. Fingerprint or face unlock. Set one up and test it. A broken sensor is a common fault.
  8. Water damage. You cannot see it easily, so be careful. If the phone has been opened or the screen has been replaced, ask why.

How to judge the battery

The battery decides how useful the phone is every day. We found no official way to read battery health across all Android brands, because it differs by maker. So test behaviour instead:

  • Note the charge level when you start. Use the phone for 10 minutes with the screen on, playing a video. If the percentage drops fast, the battery is probably worn.
  • Feel the phone while it charges. A little warmth is normal. If it gets hot, be careful.
  • Ask the seller how long the battery lasts on a normal day, and listen for an honest answer.
  • If the battery looks swollen, or the back cover is lifting, do not buy the phone.

On an iPhone, you can look in Settings, then Battery, then Battery Health. Apple says the "maximum capacity" figure compares the battery with when it was new. Apple says iPhone 14 models and earlier are designed to keep 80 percent of original capacity at 500 full charge cycles under ideal conditions. iPhone 15 models are designed for 1,000 cycles. These figures are as checked in November 2026, and real results depend on how the phone was used and charged (Apple Support).

A low figure does not mean the phone is bad, but it does mean you should spend less. If the battery is worn, you may have to pay for a replacement soon. Apple also says a message about a degraded battery is not a safety issue, but you may notice poorer battery life and performance.

What to ask the seller, and what to keep

Some questions cost nothing and tell you a lot.

  • Is this your phone? Why are you selling it?
  • Have you removed your accounts and erased the phone?
  • Has the screen, battery or any other part been replaced?
  • Do you have the box, charger and receipt?

Then protect yourself:

  • Ask for the seller's full name and phone number, and write them down. Do this politely. A seller who refuses may have a reason.
  • Ask for a receipt, even a handwritten one, that names the phone, its IMEI, the price and the date. This is common sense and not legal advice. If you need advice on a dispute, ask a qualified person.
  • Keep the box, if any, and any other papers.
  • Pay in a way that leaves a record, such as mobile money, so there is proof of the payment. Do not send money before you have the phone in your hand.
  • Meet in a busy, public place during the day. Do not go alone to a place you do not know.

A hypothetical example: say you meet a seller who will not erase the phone and tells you to "do it at home." That is a reason to walk away, because the account is still on the phone and you cannot confirm that it will be free to use. You lose nothing by leaving. You can lose a lot by staying.

If the price seems too good, take extra care. A low price is sometimes the only clue that something is wrong.

Common questions

Does the TCRA IMEI page tell me if a phone is stolen?

We could not find any such statement on the page. It lists the model, maker and frequency bands for you to compare with your phone, and it warns about fake devices. Use it to confirm the phone matches what the seller says. Do not use it as proof that the phone is clean.

What if the seller says the account lock is "not a problem"?

Treat it as a problem. Both Apple and Google say the phone needs the previous owner's account details if it was not removed. If the seller is not there to remove it, you cannot fix it yourself.

Is a cheap phone with a worn battery still a good buy?

It can be, if the price is lower to match and you are ready to replace the battery. Ask a trusted repair person what a battery replacement costs for that model before you decide. We give no prices here because they change.

Should I buy from a shop or from a person?

Either can be fine. A shop is easier to find again if there is a problem, and may give a short written warranty. A person may offer a lower price. Run the same checks in both cases.

How long should the checks take?

About ten to fifteen minutes. If the seller hurries you, slow down.

What to do next

  1. Write the checks from this post in your notes app so you can follow them in the same order every time.
  2. Before you meet a seller, charge your own phone and bring your own SIM card and a charger.
  3. Do the IMEI check, the account check and the hands-on test. If any step fails, say thank you and leave.
  4. After you buy, set a new screen lock, add your own account and make a first backup.

Buying second-hand takes patience, and your patience is the best protection you have. Take your time and you will find a phone that serves you well.

Sources and further reading

  • Verify IMEI, Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority
  • If you want to buy or get a used iPhone, iPad or Apple Watch (Activation Lock), Apple Support
  • Factory Reset Protection on Android, Google Pixel Help
  • About iPhone battery and performance (maximum capacity), Apple Support
  • Find the serial number or IMEI on your iPhone, Apple Support

item.title: Dropshipping From Tanzania: What Really Happens to an Order
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Thinking of dropshipping from Tanzania? See how one order travels, where customs, payments and returns can go wrong, and what to test first.
item.content:encoded:
Dropshipping sounds simple: you sell a product, a supplier sends it, and you never touch a box. For a reader in Tanzania, the picture gets harder once the supplier is abroad. Time, tax, payment and returns all start to matter.

This post follows one order from the first click to the doorstep. It does not say dropshipping is easy, and it does not promise any income. It also does not recommend or rank any supplier.

The short answer

You can run a dropshipping shop from Tanzania, but the risks sit mostly with you. You are the seller your customer knows. If the parcel is late, damaged or wrong, the customer blames you, not the supplier.

  • Shipping from abroad can take weeks, and the customer waits.
  • Customs and tax may apply when goods enter Tanzania. Ask before you promise a final price.
  • Some payment tools that foreign shops use are not available in Tanzania.
  • Some suppliers do not take returns, so you may lose the money.
  • Order a sample first and start with one product.

How one dropshipping order travels

Shopify, the company that makes shop software, describes dropshipping as selling products you never stock. When an order comes in, you pass it to a supplier, who ships it straight to your customer. You set the price, take the payment and answer the customer's questions.

Here is one order, step by step:

  1. A customer in Mwanza sees your post and orders a phone stand.
  2. The customer pays you, for example by mobile money.
  3. You pay the supplier abroad the supplier's price, and give them your customer's address.
  4. The supplier packs the item and hands it to a carrier.
  5. The parcel travels across borders and goes through customs in Tanzania.
  6. It reaches the customer, or it does not, or it arrives damaged.
  7. The customer writes to you.

Notice that steps 3 to 6 happen out of your sight. You do not see the item, the box or the label. You are trusting a stranger with your customer's order.

Shipping time and customs on the way into Tanzania

Shopify says shipping from overseas can be slow. Its own example is orders sent by one Chinese shipping service, which it says take 7 to 15 business days. That is an example from the company, not a promise for Tanzania. Your own orders may be faster or slower. Ask the supplier for a real delivery time to Tanzania, and test it with a sample.

Customers often expect faster delivery than that. If your page says "arrives in 3 days" and the parcel takes three weeks, you will face angry messages and refund requests. Write an honest time on every product page.

What happens at customs

We opened the Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA) page on import procedures. As checked in November 2026, it says that imports into Tanzania follow East African Community customs rules. The importer appoints a licensed clearing and forwarding agent. The documents are filed online through the Tanzania Customs Integrated System (TANCIS). Documents listed include the final invoice, a packing list and a transport document such as an airway bill.

That page describes formal imports of goods, usually done through an agent. It does not describe small courier parcels. So we cannot tell you how duty on a small parcel is worked out. Ask TRA, or the courier, before you promise a price to a customer.

TRA's VAT page says that importing taxable goods into Mainland Tanzania is subject to VAT at 18%, with normal customs procedures applying. Whether a particular small parcel pays this, and how much, depends on the goods and the route. Check with TRA.

The Tanzania Posts Corporation

If a parcel comes by post, the Tanzania Posts Corporation says on its website that parcels weigh from 3 kg to 30 kg. It says international parcels are sealed in front of a postal officer and a customs officer, and that a declaration form helps to estimate customs duty. Ask which service the supplier will use.

Shopify also warns that low-value imports can face duties and taxes, and that wrongly classified goods can cause fees and delays. Its examples are about the United States, so they are not Tanzanian rules. The lesson still holds: the customs bill can change the real cost of a product.

Getting paid and paying the supplier from Tanzania

You need a way to take money from customers and a way to pay the supplier. Both can be harder than a video tutorial makes it look.

Shopify Payments is the payment tool built into Shopify. Shopify's help page lists 41 supported countries. As checked in November 2026, Tanzania is not on the list. The page says that if your country is not listed, you need a third-party payment provider. If you plan to use a platform, check its help pages for Tanzania before you pay for anything.

For customers in Tanzania, many people pay by mobile money. Be clear about how you receive it. Our post on trust for new online sellers explains why buyers hesitate to pay first.

Paying a supplier abroad is a separate problem. We did not research the rules for sending money out of Tanzania, and we do not give any here. Ask your bank, and check the Bank of Tanzania website before you send money.

A made-up example with TSh

This example is made up to show how money can disappear. The numbers are not real prices.

ItemAmount (TSh)
Customer pays you40,000
You pay the supplier20,000
Shipping to Tanzania8,000
Payment fee2,000
What is left10,000

Here, 40,000 minus 20,000, minus 8,000, minus 2,000 leaves 10,000. That is before your phone data, advertising, and your time.

Now say the customer returns the item and the supplier refuses to take it back. You refund 40,000, so you get nothing from this sale. You have already paid 20,000 to the supplier, 8,000 for shipping and 2,000 in fees. You lose 30,000. One return like this can wipe out the profit from three good sales in this example.

Returns, complaints and who carries the loss

Shopify lists returns as a risk. It says some suppliers do not take returns and may not refund, so the store can lose money. It also says the store handles customer support, including delays and supplier mistakes.

Before you sell, ask the supplier in writing:

  • Do you accept returns? Who pays the return shipping?
  • What happens if the item arrives broken or wrong?
  • How long will you take to refund me?
  • Can you give me a tracking number for every order?

If the answers are vague, treat that as an answer. Keep the messages.

Write your own return rule on your shop page, and make sure you can honour it even if the supplier does not. Rights under Tanzanian consumer law were not part of what we checked here. Look at the Fair Competition Commission website for current rules.

Do not sell fakes

Never sell counterfeit goods or fake branded items. It harms customers, and most selling platforms ban it. If a product has a famous brand name at a very low price, think carefully, and walk away if you doubt it is genuine.

Check who you are dealing with

The Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority (TCRA) has warned about online fraud. For large purchases from foreign online merchants, it advises checking whether the merchant has an agent in the country and buying through that agent where possible. This advice is for buyers, but as a dropshipper you are also a buyer from your supplier. A supplier with no clear business name, address or contact is a warning sign. Our post on fake followers and "guaranteed sales" offers lists other offers to avoid.

Safer first steps: samples, one supplier, honest delivery times

Shopify says to order samples before listing products, and that you can sometimes ask for the sample fee to be taken off later orders. A sample shows you the real quality, the packaging and the real delivery time to Tanzania.

A careful start could look like this:

  1. Choose one small, light item that is not fragile, not branded and not regulated.
  2. Order one sample to your own address. Note the dates and any customs charge.
  3. Check the quality honestly. Would you be happy if you had paid for it?
  4. Write product pages that state the real delivery time and the full price, with no surprise costs at the door.
  5. Try a few orders from friends or family who know it is a test, and learn from the problems.
  6. Only then think about advertising.

Keep your own spending small, and do not borrow money for stock or advertising. For other starting ideas, see our list of low-cost ways to start an online business in Tanzania.

Common questions

Is dropshipping legal in Tanzania?

We did not find an official Tanzanian page that names dropshipping. The goods you import and the money you earn still fall under customs and tax rules. Ask TRA and BRELA how your business should be registered. See our post on registering a small business.

Do I need a lot of money to start?

You do not need to buy stock, but you will still pay for samples, a way to take payments, and your time. Costs and risks depend on the product, so we do not give a figure.

Can I make a steady income from it?

We cannot say. Results vary a great deal, and many shops sell little. Treat it as a test and plan for the possibility that it earns nothing.

What if the parcel never arrives?

Ask the supplier for tracking before you start. Tell the customer early, and offer a refund if the parcel is lost. Keep every message in case there is a dispute.

What to do next

  1. Write down what you would sell, and who would buy it in Tanzania.
  2. Ask a supplier the four return questions above, in writing.
  3. Ask TRA or a courier what duty and VAT could apply to a small parcel of that item.
  4. Order one sample and record the real time and cost.

A slow, careful test costs little, and what you learn from it is worth more than a fast start that ends in refunds.
