  • Shopify Payments supported countries, Shopify Help Center
  • Normal transport and parcels, Tanzania Posts Corporation
  • Import procedures, Tanzania Revenue Authority
  • Value added tax (VAT), Tanzania Revenue Authority
  • TCRA launches campaign to curb online fraud, Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority

item.title: Excel for Beginners: Simple Formulas for a Budget or Marks Sheet
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Build a small monthly budget sheet step by step. Learn SUM, AVERAGE and cell references, with the same formulas in Google Sheets. No experience needed.
item.content:encoded:
Maybe you add up your money in your head, or on the back of a receipt. That works until the month gets busy. A spreadsheet does the adding for you, never gets tired, and shows you where the money goes. Learning it costs nothing but a little time, and it is a skill that employers and shop owners use every day.

This post builds one small sheet from nothing. The steps use Excel on a computer, and we also show the same formulas for Google Sheets. Formulas are checked against Microsoft and Google help pages in November 2026. Menus differ between Excel for desktop, Excel for the web and Google Sheets, so the buttons may look a little different on your screen.

The short answer

A spreadsheet is a grid. Each box is a cell with an address like B2 (column B, row 2). A formula is a calculation you type into a cell.

  • Every formula starts with an equals sign (=).
  • =SUM(B2:B6) adds the cells from B2 down to B6.
  • =AVERAGE(B2:B6) finds the average of those cells.
  • Put numbers in cells and point formulas at the cells. Do not type the numbers inside the formula.
  • A dollar sign, as in $B$7, keeps a cell address fixed when you copy a formula.

Your first formula: cells, the equals sign and SUM

Microsoft's guide says that formulas in Excel always begin with the equals sign. To build one, select a cell, type =, then choose cells or type their addresses, add an operator such as + or -, and press Enter.

Let us make a monthly budget. This is an example, not real data. Type these in columns A and B, starting at row 1:

AB
1ItemAmount (TSh)
2Rent150000
3Food120000
4Transport45000
5Airtime and data20000
6Books15000
7Total

Type plain numbers without commas. You can add the comma display later with formatting.

Click cell B7 and type =SUM(B2:B6), then press Enter. Microsoft's page for SUM shows the same pattern, =SUM(A2:A10), which totals cells A2 to A10. The answer in B7 should be 350,000. Check it by hand: 150,000 plus 120,000 is 270,000. Add 45,000 to get 315,000. Add 20,000 to get 335,000. Add 15,000 and you reach 350,000.

You can also use the AutoSum button. Microsoft says it inserts a formula that adds a range of cells for you.

Now you can see the power. Change Food to 100000. The total changes to 330,000 by itself. You did not touch the formula.

Why not type numbers inside the formula?

You could type =150000+120000+45000+20000+15000. It gives the same answer today. But Microsoft says it is best to place constants, the fixed numbers, in their own cells, where they are easy to change and then refer to. If rent goes up, you change one cell, and every formula that uses it updates.

This is the first of two common beginner mistakes. The second is text in a number cell. Say you type 20,000 TSh with letters in cell B5. Excel sees text, not a number. Microsoft's page says SUM ignores text and adds only the numbers, so your total will be too small, and you may not notice. If you add cells with plus signs instead, such as =B2+B3+B5, Microsoft says you get a #VALUE! error when a cell contains text. Keep the amount cells to numbers only, and put words like "TSh" in the heading.

How do I find an average with AVERAGE?

An average tells you what is typical. Add the numbers, then divide by how many there are. Excel does both steps.

For the budget, click cell B8 and type =AVERAGE(B2:B6). The answer is 70,000, because 350,000 divided by 5 items is 70,000.

Now a marks example. This is a made-up list of four test scores, only to practise: 62, 70, 55 and 81. Type them in cells B2 to B5 on a new sheet. Then =SUM(B2:B5) gives 268, and =AVERAGE(B2:B5) gives 67, because 268 divided by 4 is 67.

Your school has its own rules for grades and how marks are counted. A spreadsheet only does the arithmetic. Use the grading rules your teacher gives you.

Two details from Microsoft's AVERAGE page are worth knowing. Empty cells in the range are ignored, and so is text. But a cell with a zero is counted. So if a test was not taken, leave the cell empty. Do not type 0 unless the student really scored zero.

Copy a formula down, and what does the dollar sign do?

Suppose you want to see what share of your total each item takes. In cell C2, type =B2/$B$7 and press Enter. Rent is 150,000 out of 350,000, so the answer is about 0.43.

Now copy C2 down to C6. Microsoft explains the rule. New formulas use relative references, which shift when you copy them. So B2 becomes B3, then B4, and so on, which is what you want for each item. But absolute references, written with dollar signs like $B$7, stay fixed. That keeps every row pointing at the total in B7.

If you forget the dollar signs, row 3 would divide by B8, row 4 by B9, and the answers would be wrong. Here the shares come to about 0.43, 0.34, 0.13, 0.06 and 0.04. They add up to 1, which is a good check that you did it right. Use the percent format on the column if you want to see them as percentages.

Do the same formulas work in Google Sheets?

Yes. Google's function list describes SUM as returning the sum of a series of numbers and/or cells, and AVERAGE as returning the numerical average of a dataset, ignoring text. You type =SUM(B2:B6) and =AVERAGE(B2:B6) just as in Excel.

Google Sheets is free with a Google account and works in a browser or a phone app. A free web version of Excel exists too, but it needs a Microsoft account, and what it includes can change, so check Microsoft's page. If you worry about data costs, read how to save mobile data when studying online.

Common questions

Why does my cell show the formula instead of the answer?

Usually the cell was set to text, or there is a space before the equals sign. Make sure the formula starts with = and nothing before it.

Why is my total smaller than expected?

Check for numbers stored as text, such as a value with letters in it. SUM skips text.

Do I need to buy Excel?

Not to learn these ideas. Google Sheets covers all of them. Check Microsoft's site for what Excel plans cost today, because we do not list prices.

What is a range?

A range is a block of cells, written with a colon. B2:B6 means B2 down to B6.

What to do next

  1. Make the budget sheet above with your own real items for one month.
  2. Add a line for money coming in, and a formula that subtracts your total spending. For example, if you receive 400,000 and spend 350,000, the answer is 50,000.
  3. Try the marks example with your own scores, and check one answer by hand.
  4. If you run a small stall, the same sheet can track daily sales. Our post on how to price your products pairs well with it.

A small sheet you built yourself is a real step forward. Start with five rows, and let it grow when you are ready.

Sources and further reading

  • Overview of formulas in Excel, Microsoft Support
  • SUM function, Microsoft Support
  • AVERAGE function, Microsoft Support
  • Google Sheets function list, Google Docs Editors Help

item.title: Facebook Account Hacked? What to Do, Step by Step
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Posts you did not write, or a login that no longer works? Follow a calm order of steps to secure your Facebook account, and learn how to lock it down.
item.content:encoded:
You open Facebook and see a post you never wrote. Or your password suddenly stops working. Your stomach drops, and you want to fix it in one minute. Take a breath. This is a common problem, and there is a clear order of steps that helps. This post gives you that order.

The short answer

If you think someone else is using your Facebook account, act in this order. Speed matters, but order matters more.

  • Use a phone or computer you have logged in from before, on your usual home or work network.
  • Follow the recovery steps that Meta links from its Safety Center page, and use the form for a compromised account.
  • Once you are in, check "Where You're Logged In" and log out every device you do not know.
  • Change your password to a new, long and unique one, and turn on two-factor authentication.
  • Warn your friends that nobody should send money or codes to "you" until you say you are back.

We cannot promise that every account can be recovered. What you can do is follow the official route and avoid the traps around it.

Signs your account may have been hacked

Not every strange thing means a hack. Sometimes a friend tags you in a post, or you forget a password. But these signs are worth taking seriously:

  • Posts, messages or friend requests you did not make.
  • A password that stops working although you typed it correctly.
  • Emails or alerts about a login from a place or device you do not know.
  • Changes to your name, birthday, email address or phone number that you did not make.
  • Friends telling you that you sent them a strange link or asked them for money.

Meta's Safety Center page says that if your account is hacked or compromised, you should "secure it immediately". It links to recovery steps and to a form for reporting a compromised Facebook account. As checked in November 2026, that is the starting point we recommend.

Do these steps first

If you can still log in, work through this list slowly. Do not close the page halfway.

  1. Use a safe device. Use a phone or computer you trust and have used for Facebook before. Do not use a shared computer at a cyber cafe if you can avoid it.
  2. Open the Meta Safety Center page (the link is in the sources below) and follow its link for hacked accounts. Type the address yourself or use the link in this post. Do not tap a link in a message or email that says "Facebook Security".
  3. Run Security Checkup. Meta's page recommends it as the place to review and add security to your account. You must be logged in to use it.
  4. Open "Security and Login" in your settings and find "Where You're Logged In". This lists devices that have recently used your account. Log out any device you do not recognise.
  5. Change your password. Use a long one that you have never used anywhere else. The next section and our password post explain how.
  6. Turn on two-factor authentication. Meta says it adds an extra layer of protection when someone tries to get into your account from a new computer, phone or tablet.
  7. Turn on login alerts. Meta says you can be alerted when someone tries to log in from a device it does not recognise. The alert shows the device and where it is.
  8. Check your email. If Facebook sent you messages about a change to your account, read them carefully. Do not tap links in them. Open Facebook yourself and look at the settings there.
  9. Remove things you did not do. Delete posts you did not write and apologise briefly to anyone who got a strange message.

Menu names change from time to time and may look different in Swahili or on an older phone. We describe settings by name, as checked in November 2026. If a name is slightly different on your screen, look for the closest match.

If you cannot get in

This is the scariest case. You type your password and it says no. Your email may have been changed too.

Do not try ten random passwords in a row. Do not install a "recovery app". Instead:

  • Start from a device you have used before for Facebook, if you can. It is the safest place to begin.
  • Use the recovery steps and the compromised-account form linked from the Meta Safety Center page.
  • Check the email account that was linked to Facebook. If you cannot get into that either, recover your email first, using that email company's own help page.
  • Be patient. Recovery can take time, and not every case ends the way we would like.

One more warning, and it is our own editorial advice. After a hack, people on social media will offer to "get your account back" for a fee. Do not pay them. A stranger who needs your password, a code or your money is often the next scammer. The only route that works is the one Meta itself provides, and it is free.

What to tell your friends and family

A hacked account is often used to trick the people who trust you. A message from "you" says, "I am stuck, please send TSh 50,000 on mobile money, I will pay you back." Your friend sees your name and your photo, and may want to help.

So tell people quickly, by phone call or WhatsApp, or from another account if you have one:

  • "My Facebook was hacked. Do not send any money or codes to anyone in my name."
  • "If I ask for money, call me on my phone first."
  • "Do not tap any link that came from my account."

If someone already sent money, tell them to contact their mobile money operator at once. We have a separate post on how to check an AI voice or video scam, and the same call-back habit works here.

Lock it down so it does not happen again

Most hacks begin with a stolen or reused password, or with a trick that gets you to type your password into a fake page. These habits make the next attempt much harder.

HabitWhy it helps
A different password for every important accountOne leak cannot open the others
Two-factor authentication on FacebookA stolen password alone is not enough
Login alerts onYou hear about strange logins early
Check "Where You're Logged In" now and thenYou can remove old or unknown devices
Open Facebook from the app or by typing the addressFake login pages are a common trap
Never share a code you receive by SMSCodes are meant only for you

Meta's own page also says to use a different password for each account, not to share passwords, and not to store them where others can find them. Meta suggests at least eight characters; we suggest much longer, because longer passwords are harder to guess. See our post on strong passwords and password managers.

If you also use WhatsApp, protect it too. Our post on two-step verification for WhatsApp shows how.

Common questions

Should I report a hacked account to the police?

TCRA's FAQ advises reporting fraud to a police station, where you can get an RB number and an investigator. We are not lawyers, so ask the police how they treat your case. If money was lost, a police report can help. Keep screenshots of the strange posts and messages.

Can I just delete my account and start again?

You can, but first try to secure and recover it. Deleting does not stop a scammer from using your name, and a fake new account can still be made. If a fake account pretends to be you, Meta's Safety Center says to report it.

Will two-factor authentication stop everything?

No. It makes a hack much harder, but you can still be tricked into giving away a code. Never share a code with anyone, even someone who sounds friendly or official.

My friend's account sent me a strange link. What should I do?

Do not open it. Tell your friend by phone that their account may be hacked. You can also report the message inside Facebook.

What to do next

  1. Today, check "Where You're Logged In" and log out every device you do not know.
  2. Change your Facebook password to a long, new one and turn on two-factor authentication and login alerts.
  3. Tell three close friends or relatives how to recognise a message that is not really from you.
  4. Make a note of your recovery email and phone number, and keep them up to date.

A hacked account feels personal, but it does not mean you were careless or foolish. You acted, and that is what counts.

Sources and further reading

  • Meta Safety Center: Security tools, Meta
  • Frequent asked questions on customer and consumer affairs, TCRA

item.title: Fake Followers and 'Guaranteed Sales' Offers: Don't Fall for Them
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Offered 10,000 followers or a guaranteed first place on Google? Here is what Meta and Google say, the warning signs, and what to do if you already paid.
item.content:encoded:
You open your shop's page and see 200 followers. A rival down the road has 20,000. Then a message arrives: "We can fix that for a few thousand shillings." It is easy to feel small at that moment, and easy to say yes. This post is here to slow you down for five minutes.

The short answer

No, it is not safe to buy followers or to pay anyone who says they can promise you sales or a first place on Google. The platforms themselves say so, and nobody outside those companies controls the results.

  • Meta's rules prohibit buying engagement such as likes, shares and views, and buying accounts or pages.
  • Google says no one can guarantee a number one ranking.
  • A big follower count does not pay your rent. Customers do.
  • Honest, slow work (good photos, quick replies, happy customers who tell others) is cheaper and safer.
  • If you have already paid, stop, protect your accounts and keep your records. The last section tells you how.

Why do these offers feel so tempting?

Many small owners in Tanzania sell through WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook. A page with few followers can look new or risky to a stranger. So a seller who says "20,000 followers by tomorrow" is selling relief from that worry.

The worry is real. The fix is not. A follower who never reads your posts will never buy your tomatoes, shoes or phone covers. Think about it this way: if you paid TSh 20,000 for numbers on a screen, what would you have in your hand next week? A bigger number, and no new customer.

The same pressure shows up in a second form. Someone promises "guaranteed sales" or "guaranteed first place on Google". It sounds like a business partner. It is usually a promise nobody can keep.

What do Meta and Google actually say?

We checked these pages in November 2026. Policies change, so open the links in "Sources and further reading" for the current wording.

Meta (Facebook and Instagram)

Meta's Spam policy lists, among the things it prohibits, attempting to or successfully selling, buying or exchanging for engagement, such as likes, shares and views. It also prohibits selling, buying or exchanging platform assets such as accounts, groups and pages.

That means a seller of followers is offering something the platform does not allow, and a buyer is taking part in it. Meta's policy tells you what is not allowed. We could not confirm from the policy what happens to a particular account, so we will not guess. The honest point is simple: you would be building your shop on something the platform says you may not do.

Meta's fraud and scams policy also names things like offers of unrealistic financial reward for unclear or minimal effort, and offers where returns are guaranteed or risk-free. It lists advance fees (a promise of money for a payment up front) and failing to deliver a service after you have paid. These match the patterns in most "growth" scams.

Google

Google's own page on whether you need an SEO helper is blunt: "No one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google." It adds that if someone guarantees that their changes will give you first place, you should find someone else.

Google also warns about companies that contact you out of the blue, about secrecy, and about claims of a special relationship with Google or a "priority submit". Nobody can buy a private door into search results.

What are the warning signs before you pay?

Look for these. One sign is a reason to ask more questions. Two or three together is a reason to walk away.

  • A guarantee. "Guaranteed sales", "guaranteed first page", "guaranteed 10,000 followers". Real marketing has no guarantees.
  • Unrealistic speed or size. Big results for very little work or money.
  • Pressure. "The price goes up tonight." "Only three places left."
  • Payment first, details later. Especially if they want full payment by mobile money before showing any work.
  • Secrecy. They will not explain what they will actually do.
  • A message out of the blue. A direct message or email you did not ask for.
  • They ask for your password. Never share it. Legitimate help does not need your login.
  • They ask for full control of your accounts. Google says to give an SEO helper read access only to your Search Console, at the start, and not write access.
  • They want you to link to their site or place their links on your pages.
  • No real examples. They cannot show past work you can check yourself.

Questions to ask any marketing helper

Google suggests asking an SEO adviser questions like these, and they work for any helper:

  1. Can you show me examples of your previous work, and let me check them myself?
  2. What results do you expect, and over what time?
  3. What exactly will you do on my accounts and pages?
  4. Will I keep full control of my accounts and my website?
  5. What happens if nothing improves?

A good helper answers calmly in plain words. A scammer gets annoyed, vague or fast.

Can I be punished for what I say in my own adverts?

This section is about your own claims, not about the sellers. It is general information, not legal advice. For your own case, ask a lawyer.

The Fair Competition Act, 2003 has rules on honest trading. In the copy published by WIPO Lex, section 15 says nobody shall, in trade, engage in conduct that is misleading or deceptive or likely to mislead or deceive. Section 16 lists false or misleading representations about goods and services, including about price, quality, and guarantees. Section 20 covers false or misleading statements about the profitability or risk of a business activity. The section numbers may differ in a later edition of the Act, so check the current text.

What does this mean for you? Do not copy a seller's tricks. Do not tell customers you have "50,000 happy customers" if the number is bought. Do not promise results you cannot control. A small, true claim ("open since 2021, delivery within Dar es Salaam") is stronger and safer.

What can I do instead that actually works?

Slow methods cost little and build something you own.

  • Ask happy customers to share your page. One real customer who tells a neighbour is worth more than a hundred empty accounts.
  • Post real pictures of your real products with the price and where to find you.
  • Reply quickly. Many buyers decide by how fast you answer a question.
  • Give your page the same name as your shop sign so people can find you.
  • Keep a simple list of customers who agreed to hear from you. The post on SMS and email marketing consent explains how to do that fairly.
  • Be patient. Real trust grows over weeks and months.

Say you spend TSh 20,000 on printed price cards and a clear sign instead. Customers who walk past can see what you sell and what it costs. That is a real result you can see, and no seller can take it away.

What if I have already paid or shared a password?

Many people have done this. It is not stupid, it is human. Do these steps in order.

  1. Stop paying. Do not send "one more fee" to fix the problem.
  2. Change your password now on the account involved, and on any other account that uses the same password. Use a long password you have not used elsewhere.
  3. Turn on two-step login if the app offers it.
  4. Check who has access. Remove any person or app you do not know from your page roles and connected apps.
  5. Keep proof. Save messages, receipts and mobile money confirmations. Take screenshots.
  6. Tell the platform if your account is at risk, using its help pages.
  7. Ask your mobile money provider whether they have a way to report a fraud.
  8. Report it. Google's page says that for a company in another country, you can file a complaint at econsumer.gov. For a seller inside Tanzania, ask the police or a lawyer how to proceed.
  9. Tell a friend in business. Scammers rely on silence.

Do not expect to get money back. We cannot promise that, and you should be careful about anyone who says they can recover it for a fee.

Common questions

Will buying followers help my sales?

We found no reason to think so. A follower who is not a real, interested customer will not buy. Also, it is against Meta's rules to buy engagement.

Is it wrong to hire someone to help with my page?

No. Many honest people help small shops with photos, writing and posting. The warning signs above separate them from scammers. Start with a small, clear task and pay for work you can see.

Can anyone really get me to the top of Google?

Google says no one can guarantee it. Honest helpers can improve how clear your pages are. Nobody can promise a place.

I got a message offering to "manage" my page. Is it real?

Treat it as unsafe until you can check who it is. Do not give a password. Look at the warning signs above, and ask for past work you can verify yourself.

What to do next

  1. Open your page and look at it as a stranger would. Is the name clear? Are prices, location and a contact number easy to find?
  2. Ask three happy customers this week to share your page or leave a kind comment.
  3. If someone has already offered you "followers" or "guaranteed sales", save the message and do not reply with money.

Slow and honest is not the weaker path. It is the one that is still standing next year.

Sources and further reading

  • Spam, Community Standards, Meta Transparency Center
  • Fraud and scams policy, Meta Transparency Center
  • Do you need an SEO expert, Google Search Central
  • Fair Competition Act, 2003, WIPO Lex (PDF)

item.title: Fake Job Offers in Tanzania: Warning Signs and What to Do
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: How to spot a fake job or internship offer, a five-minute check before you reply, and what to do if someone asked you to pay or you shared documents.
item.content:encoded:
When you badly need work, a message that says "You have been selected" can feel like an answer to prayer. That hope is exactly what scammers use. This post helps you slow down, check, and protect your money and your documents.

The short answer

A real employer does not ask you to pay to get a job, to be shortlisted or to attend an interview. If someone asks for money before you start work, treat the offer as fake until an official source proves otherwise. Stop, do not pay, and check with the organisation using contact details you find yourself.

  • Never pay for the promise of a job, a "form", a "medical", a "uniform" or a "training".
  • Do not trust a job that you did not apply for, especially one that arrives by SMS or WhatsApp.
  • Public service jobs are applied for through the official recruitment portal, not through a person.
  • Check the offer in another place before you reply.
  • If you paid, act quickly and report it.

Warning signs of a fake job offer

Several official bodies describe the same pattern. The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says honest employers do not charge applicants, and its advice is simple: do not pay for the promise of a job. The International Labour Organization (ILO) says in its fair recruitment principles that no recruitment fees or related costs should be charged to workers or job seekers. Those principles are not a law, but they show a common global standard.

This is general advice from outside Tanzania, and it matches the local pattern. Watch for these signs:

  • They ask for money. Fees for registration, shortlisting, interview, training, a uniform or a "security". The FTC lists fees for kits, training and certificates as a warning sign.
  • You never applied. A surprise offer for a job you did not apply for is a reason to be careful.
  • Big pay for little work. The FTC says offers of high earnings for little effort are almost certainly scams.
  • Hiring only by chat. No office, no interview, no written job description, only a chat app or a phone call.
  • A pressure clock. "Pay today or lose the post."
  • A cheque that needs a refund. The FTC describes fake cheque scams, where a new "employer" sends a payment and asks you to send part of it back or buy something. The cheque later bounces and you lose your own money.
  • Contacts that do not check out. Free email addresses for a large organisation, a phone that does not answer, a website that has disappeared.
  • Placement firms that charge up front. The FTC says honest placement firms are usually paid by the employer, not by you.
  • Requests for ID, bank or mobile money details before any real hiring step.

One more point: a real organisation can still be pretended. A fake advert may use a real company's name. That is why checking matters. We do not name any company here, because a fake message does not mean the company did anything wrong.

What real recruitment looks like

Real recruitment leaves a trail you can check.

For jobs in the central public service, the vacancy announcement we read in November 2026 said that all applications must be sent through the official recruitment portal and that applications sent through any other means will not be considered. It also said only shortlisted candidates will be told of the interview date. It did not mention a fee. So a person who says "give me money and I will put your name in" is not following the official route. See our guide to applying through the Ajira Portal.

For private employers, you can usually expect:

  • An advert on the employer's own website or official page
  • A clear job title, duties and qualifications
  • A named contact and a real address
  • A written interview invitation, and an interview at a real office or on a known video platform
  • A written contract before you start work, with no payment from you

Some organisations have published their own warnings. World Vision Tanzania has one that says it does not charge for recruitment, but we could not open that page when we checked in November 2026, so we do not quote it. If you think an offer is from a big organisation, find its official careers page and look for a warning or a list of real vacancies.

A five-minute check before you reply

Take these steps before you send a document, a payment or even your phone number.

  1. Pause. Do not answer straight away. Tell a trusted person, as the FTC advises.
  2. Find the employer yourself. Search for the organisation's own website or official page. Do not use links or numbers sent in the message.
  3. Look for the same advert there. If the vacancy is not on the official page, ask the organisation using the contact details you found yourself.
  4. Search the offer. Type the company name or the person's name with the word "scam" or "complaint". The FTC suggests this check.
  5. Read the message again. Does it ask for money, ID, bank or mobile money details? If so, stop.
  6. Look at how they want to talk. Real interviews do not happen only through voice notes.
  7. Do not send money, even a small amount. A small fee is a test. If you pay once, they will ask again.

If the offer passes all these steps, continue carefully. If you are not sure, you can wait. A real job will still be there tomorrow.

Calls and messages that pretend to be a ministry

The Prime Minister's Office, Labour, Employment and Relations published a public notice on 15 October 2026. We looked at the notice on its website. It warned about fraudulent calls from people pretending to be staff of that office. The callers were contacting people who had applied for work permits, appeals and exemptions, and demanding money with promises to speed up their applications.

That notice is about work permits, not about job vacancies, so we do not claim it covers other jobs. But the pattern is the same one to look for in any government matter:

  • The office said those callers are not its employees.
  • It said it does not give decisions about work permits, appeals or exemptions by telephone. It says decisions are published on its official website.
  • It asked the public to ignore such calls and to report similar incidents to the office, using the contacts on the notice. We do not print the numbers here. Please take them from the notice on the official site, www.kazi.go.tz.

The lesson is useful for any office. An official body does not need your money to process a case, and it does not give you results by a surprise phone call. If a caller says they are from a ministry, end the call and contact the ministry using the details on its own website.

What to do if you already paid or shared documents

First, do not feel ashamed. Scammers are practised, and many careful people have been caught. Act in this order:

  1. Stop all payments. Do not send more money to "release" what you paid.
  2. Contact your mobile money provider or bank straight away. Tell them what happened. The FTC advises contacting the company you used to send money and asking whether it can be reversed. We cannot say that reversal will be possible in Tanzania, but a quick call is always worth it.
  3. Keep the evidence. Save messages, receipts, numbers and screenshots. Do not delete the chat.
  4. Report it. Use the reporting contacts of the organisation being copied, and the police. For a scam that pretends to be a government office, use the contacts on the official notice. The FTC runs its own reporting page, but that is for US cases.
  5. Protect your identity. If you sent copies of your ID or certificates, watch for strange calls or messages, and change passwords on email and mobile money accounts that you linked to them.
  6. Warn others. Tell your friends and family group, without naming private people.

We are not lawyers, so for legal advice ask a qualified person or an official office.

For internships, see how to find an internship in Tanzania. For online freelance gigs, which have their own scam patterns, see our guide to freelancing online from Tanzania.

Common questions

Is it normal to pay for a medical test before I start a job?

A job offer should not depend on a payment to the person offering the job. If a medical check is needed, ask the employer in writing, and verify the request with the organisation using contacts you found yourself.

Can a real recruiter charge a fee?

The ILO principle says no recruitment fees or related costs should be charged to job seekers. The FTC says honest placement firms are usually paid by the employer. Treat any up-front fee as a red flag.

I got a job offer on WhatsApp. Is it always fake?

Not always, but a job offer with no interview, no written contract and a request for money is very likely fake. Check it using the five-minute list above.

Who can I ask if I am not sure?

Ask the organisation using official contact details, a teacher, a careers office at your school, or an adult you trust.

What to do next

  1. Read your messages again and look for any request for money or ID.
  2. Do the five-minute check on any offer you are considering.
  3. Save the official website of the organisations you want to work for.
  4. Share this post with a friend who is job hunting.

Hope is not a weakness. It just needs a little protection, and now you know how to give it some.

Sources and further reading

  • Public notice, 15 October 2026, Prime Minister's Office, Labour, Employment and Relations
  • Job scams, Federal Trade Commission (US)
  • General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment, International Labour Organization
  • Vacancy announcement, 13 October 2026, Public Service Recruitment Secretariat

item.title: Fake Payment Messages: How Sellers Avoid Mobile Money Scams
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Learn one simple habit that protects your goods and your money: confirm payment in your own wallet, then hand over the item. Includes what to do if you were tricked.
item.content:encoded:
You packed the order with care. The buyer says "I have paid" and shows you a message. Then you wait, and the money never comes. Every seller fears that moment, and it hurts because the work was real. This post gives you a calm routine that makes it much harder for it to happen to you.

The short answer

Never hand over goods because of a message or a screenshot. Hand them over only when you have seen the money in your own mobile money wallet or bank app.

  • A message is only text. Anyone can type or edit one, so it proves nothing by itself.
  • Open your own wallet, or dial your network's balance menu yourself, and check that the money is there.
  • Do not rush because the buyer is in a hurry. Pressure is a warning sign.
  • Never send money back to a caller or buyer because they ask you to.
  • If something goes wrong, tell your network, report the scam message, and report to the police.

Why a message is not payment

When a payment is real, the money is in your account. The message is only a notice about it. A notice can be copied, changed or sent by someone pretending to be the network. It can also be a screenshot, and a screenshot is only a picture.

So the check never changes: look at your own balance, in your own wallet, on your own phone. Do not tap a link inside a message to "confirm". Open the app or the menu yourself.

Jiji, the classifieds site, gives the same kind of warning in its safety tips. It says to watch for fake payment services and requests for fees, and to avoid anything that looks too good to be true. That page is written mainly for buyers, but the lesson works for sellers too: if you cannot verify a payment yourself, do not treat it as received.

The tricks sellers meet

We could not find an official Tanzanian page that lists the exact scripts scammers use, so we will not claim to know which one is most common. What we can say is that these pressure points appear again and again when people talk about selling online. Treat each as a reason to slow down.

  • Pressure. "I am late, please send the item now, the money is coming." A real buyer can wait two minutes while you check.
  • The screenshot. The buyer sends a picture of a payment. It may be old, edited or from someone else's phone.
  • The message from "the network". A text arrives that looks official but comes from an ordinary number or contains a link. Your network does not need you to release goods for it.
  • The "send it back" request. Someone says they paid by mistake and asks you to return the money. If the money is not in your wallet, there is nothing to return, and you would be sending your own.
  • A deal that is too good. A very large order from a stranger, with a request to pay extra fees or use an unusual transfer service, is a reason to stop.

Are these a big problem? Tanzania's regulator, TCRA, runs a public campaign against phone fraud called Sitapeliki. The Daily News reported in July 2025 that TCRA data showed mobile money fraud cases fell from 17,152 in March to 13,837 in June 2025. That is fewer, but still many. The same article advises people to change their PIN often and to check the recipient's details before sending money.

A five-step check before you hand over goods

Use the same steps for every sale, even when the buyer is a friend of a friend. A routine feels rude only the first time.

  1. Say your rule early. Write it in your chat or on your shop page: "I release goods after the money shows in my wallet." Honest buyers understand.
  2. Give the right number. If you have a merchant or business number, give that. Check each digit before you send it.
  3. Check your own wallet. Open your app or dial the network's menu yourself. Look at the balance and the transaction list. Do not use a link from the buyer.
  4. Match the amount and the name. The full amount must be there, not less. If the name shown is odd, ask why.
  5. Only then hand over the goods. If you are not sure, wait. A real payment will still be there in an hour.

If you want to learn how to set up a proper business number, read our guide to mobile money for business.

If someone asks you to send money

Never send money to a person you do not know. TCRA says this plainly in its public advice. It also says not to follow instructions from unknown callers, not to click links from people you do not know, and not to reply to prize or emergency stories.

Say a stranger calls and says they sent you money by mistake. They ask you to send it back at once. Do not do it from the phone call. Check your wallet first. If the money is really there, ask your network on 100 how to handle it. If it is not there, you have just been saved from a loss.

If you have been tricked

It is not your fault that a scammer lied. Act quickly and calmly, in this order.

  1. Call your network on 100. TCRA tells people to contact their service provider by dialling 100. Say what happened and give the time, number and amount. Yas says that for a wrong transaction you should call customer care on 100. Yas also says its self-reversal tool works only within 30 minutes of the transaction, so speed matters. We only opened Yas's page, so check with your own network what it can do.
  2. Report the scam message. TCRA says to text the word "Fraud" to 15040. Its Swahili FAQ names the word "UTAPELI" for the same number, and Yas says "FRAUD". The word may change, so follow the instructions in the reply you get. As checked in November 2026, TCRA says reported numbers are passed to law enforcement agencies.
  3. Report to the police. TCRA's FAQ says to report fraud at a police station, where you can get an RB number (the police report number) and an investigator.
  4. Keep proof. Save messages, call times, numbers, receipts and your wallet statement. Do not delete the chat.
  5. Use the complaint route if you get no answer. For complaints that are not crime, TCRA's FAQ says to complain to your provider first. If there is no reply within 30 days, or you are not happy with it, you can take it to TCRA with proof of your complaint. The same FAQ says mobile money services are supervised by the Bank of Tanzania.

TCRA's toll-free line is 0800 008272. Phone numbers can change, so check the TCRA website before you call.

Safer ways to sell

  • Pay after inspection. Jiji advises meeting in a public place or using payment on delivery, so the buyer inspects and pays when satisfied. For you as a seller, this means money changes hands while both people are present, and you can check your wallet on the spot.
  • Do not ship on a promise. Jiji says it recommends no prepayments. If you must ship to another town, wait for confirmed money first.
  • Keep your own records. Write each sale in a notebook: date, item, amount, the buyer's number. Our post on simple business records shows an easy way.
  • Be honest in your own ads. Clear listings bring fewer arguments. See our guide on how to earn customer trust as a new online seller.

Protect your own SIM and PIN

Your wallet is only as safe as your PIN and your SIM.

  • Never tell anyone your PIN. Jiji's safety page says the same about codes and passwords. No honest network worker, buyer or "agent" needs it.
  • Change your PIN from time to time, as the Daily News article advises.
  • TCRA says you can dial *106# and follow the steps to see the SIM cards registered in your name. If you see a number you do not know, ask your provider to remove it.
  • Do not lend your phone with the wallet open.

Common questions

Can I trust a payment screenshot?

No. A screenshot is only a picture and can be old or edited. Trust only the balance and the transaction list in your own wallet or app.

The buyer says the money is "pending". What should I do?

Wait. Tell the buyer politely that you release the goods after the money shows in your wallet. A real payment does not need you to hurry.

Should I ever send money back?

Not on a caller's request. First confirm in your own wallet that the money arrived. If it did and you think it was a mistake, ask your network on 100 what to do.

Is reporting worth it?

Yes. TCRA says reported numbers are passed on for investigation, and your report may help other sellers. It also gives your network and the police a record.

What to do next

  1. Write your payment rule in one sentence and put it in your shop chat or description.
  2. Practise finding the transaction list in your wallet, so you can do it in seconds.
  3. Save 100, 15040 and the TCRA line in your phone.
  4. Share this routine with anyone who helps you sell.

Careful sellers are not unfriendly, they are the ones who are still in business next year. One small check keeps your hard work safe.

Sources and further reading

  • TCRA launches campaign to curb online fraud, Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority
  • Frequently asked questions on customer and consumer affairs, Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority
  • Consumer FAQs, Yas Tanzania
  • Safety tips for buyers, Jiji Tanzania
  • Mobile money scam attempts decline as Sitapeliki campaign bears fruit, Daily News

item.title: Free Games for Low-End Android Phones: How to Pick Safe Ones
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: How to choose free Android games for a phone with little memory and storage, read the age rating, ads and purchase labels, and spot costly "free" games.
item.content:encoded:
A cheap phone can still be a good place to play. You only need to pick games that suit it, and to read a few lines on the Play Store page before you press Install. This post shows you how, and uses four real listings as examples.

The short answer

Choose games that work offline, show no "Contains ads" label and carry an age rating that fits the player. Read the page first, then install. Keep some free storage so the phone does not slow down.

  • Check how much storage your phone has free before you download anything.
  • Look for the "Offline" tag if you do not want to spend data.
  • Read the age rating, then read the line under it. It names what earned the rating.
  • Look for "Contains ads" and "In-app purchases" under the game name.
  • A simple-looking game can still carry ads, random items and a high rating.

What counts as a low-end phone, and how to check yours

There is no official line. In this post, a low-end phone means one with little memory (RAM) and little storage, so it is slow when many apps are open and the storage fills up fast.

Games feel slow on such a phone for two common reasons. The phone has too little free storage, or the game asks for more than the phone can give. We could not find a publisher figure for the memory these games need, so we do not name one. Watch how the game behaves on your phone instead.

Check your free storage like this. Google's Android help describes these steps, and some need Android 14 or later, so your menu may look different.

  1. Open Settings, tap Storage, then tap Free up space.
  2. Look through the groups and remove files you no longer need.
  3. Uninstall apps you do not use. You can install them again later.
  4. If an app is slow, you can use Clear cache. It removes temporary data and the app may load slower the next time.

Be careful with Clear storage. It deletes all of an app's data, so a game could lose your saved progress.

Free games that run light, with their Play Store age ratings

Here are four listings we opened on Google Play. The ratings, labels and tags below are as shown in November 2026. They depend on your country and can change, so check your own Play Store before you install.

GameRating shownAds and purchases shownOffline
Shattered Pixel Dungeon7+ (mild violence, fear)In-app purchases label, no "Contains ads" labelOffline tag
Mindustry7+ (mild violence)No ads or purchases labelOffline tag
Simon Tatham's Puzzles7+ (mild violence)No ads or purchases labelOffline tag
Hill Climb Racing16+Contains ads, in-app purchases (includes random items)Playable offline

A few notes on each one.

Shattered Pixel Dungeon is a dungeon-crawling role-playing game. The listing says it is a traditional roguelike where every game is different, and it carries an in-app purchases label.

Mindustry is a factory-building and tower defence game. Its listing also advertises online multiplayer and public servers. If you use those parts, you use data and you meet other players. The single-player campaign is the part you can play offline.

Simon Tatham's Puzzles is a collection of 40 logic puzzles. The developer's description says it will always be free, with no ads, and playable offline. It is a quiet choice for a very small phone.

Hill Climb Racing is the one to learn from. It looks like a child's game, and the description says it is playable offline. Yet the Play Store page we opened shows "Contains ads", in-app purchases including random items, and a 16+ rating. Why 16+ for a driving game? The page links the rating to the random-item purchases, and you can read that line yourself on the listing.

We did not test how any of these games run on a specific phone, so we make no promise about speed. Try one, and uninstall it if it lags.

How to read a Play Store page before you install

Take thirty seconds to read these parts, in this order.

  1. The labels under the game name. Look for "Contains ads" and "In-app purchases".
  2. The age rating. It appears as "Rated for 7+", "Rated for 16+" and so on. Tap it to see the reason line, such as "Mild Violence" or "In-Game Purchases (Includes Random Items)".
  3. The tags near the bottom. An "Offline" tag means the game can be played without internet. A game with online play often still says so in its description.
  4. The developer's name. A known developer with a clear page is safer than a name you cannot find anywhere.
  5. The description. Look for words about ads, purchases and multiplayer or chat.

What the age numbers mean here

In some countries a local rating body sets the age number. Google says that in places without a participating rating authority, a generic IARC rating is shown instead, in steps of 3+, 7+, 12+, 16+ and 18+. The page does not name Tanzania, so we cannot say which system your phone shows. We can say this about the generic steps:

  • 3+ allows comical or fantasy-style violence but no bad language.
  • 7+ may include mildly frightening content and mild, non-realistic violence.
  • 12+ allows fantasy violence, mild language and simulated gambling.
  • 16+ allows realistic violence, strong language and some other adult themes.

For the full picture, including parental controls, read our post on game age ratings and parental controls.

What "free" really costs: ads, purchases and random items

Most free games earn money in one of three ways. None is hidden if you read the page, but they are easy to miss when you are in a hurry.

  • Ads. They use your data and your time. On a slow phone, they can also make the game stutter. Games with a "Contains ads" label show them.
  • In-app purchases. Some are a single payment to unlock extras. Others sell coins or boosts again and again.
  • Random items. Here you pay without knowing what you will get. Google Play marks these on the page, as it does for Hill Climb Racing. We suggest children avoid games with this label, and the Hill Climb Racing page itself says you can disable in-app purchases in your device settings.

If a young player uses your phone, look at the purchase controls in your device settings. Our post above explains the parental controls.

Be careful with chat and strangers

Some games let players talk to strangers. If a game has open chat, treat it as a place on the internet, not as a toy. Do not share your name, school, phone number or location. We do not recommend such games for young children unless an adult sits nearby.

Install only from the Play Store

Never download a game from a file-sharing site, an APK link or a "modded" version. These can carry malware, and they take away the checks that the store page gives you. If a game is not on Google Play for your phone, leave it.

Common questions

Do free games cost data to play?

An offline game does not need data once it is installed. Downloading and updating the game still uses data, so do that on Wi-Fi if you can. See our guide on saving mobile data while playing games for the settings.

How do I free up space for a new game?

Go to Settings, then Storage, then Free up space, and remove files and apps you do not need. Google's help page lists these steps. Move photos and videos to a computer or a backup if you want to keep them.

Is a game safe for my child if it is rated 7+?

A 7+ rating means mild, non-realistic violence or mildly frightening content. It does not mean the game is free of ads or purchases, so read the labels too. You know your child best, so play it with them first.

Why does the same game show a different rating on another phone?

Ratings and labels depend on the country and on updates to the game. We checked in November 2026, and what you see can differ. Trust the page on your own phone.

What to do next

  1. Check your free storage in Settings, then Storage, and clear what you do not need.
  2. Pick one game from the table, or a similar one, and read its Play Store page before you install.
  3. Play it for a few days. If it lags or shows too many ads, uninstall it and try another.
  4. Check the purchase and parental controls if children use the phone.

A small phone can still give you many good hours of play, and a careful choice is the first step.

Sources and further reading

  • Free up storage space on your Android device, Google Android Help
  • Content ratings on Google Play, Google Play Console Help
  • Shattered Pixel Dungeon, Google Play
  • Mindustry, Google Play
  • Simon Tatham's Puzzles, Google Play
  • Hill Climb Racing, Google Play

item.title: Free Video Editors: DaVinci Resolve, CapCut and Shotcut Compared
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Compare three free video editors by what they cost, what they limit and what their own terms say about your videos, music and effects, as read in November 2026.
item.content:encoded:
You have clips on your phone: a wedding, a shop opening, a school event, or a short video to promote your business. Now you want to cut them together. Many people pick the editor that looks easiest and only later learn what "free" really allowed. This post helps you choose with your eyes open.

We compare three free choices, DaVinci Resolve, CapCut and Shotcut, using each maker's own pages. Everything below is as checked in November 2026. We do not list prices or version numbers, because they change. Always read the maker's page before you decide.

The short answer

All three can be used without paying, but "free" means different things.

  • Shotcut describes itself as a free, open source, cross-platform video editor.
  • DaVinci Resolve has a free version, and a paid Studio version with extra tools.
  • CapCut has free features and paid ones, and its terms have rules about music, templates and commercial use.
  • If you will post only for fun, any of them can work.
  • If you will earn money from the video, read the licence for every music track, effect and template first.

What can "free" mean?

There are three common meanings.

Open source. Anyone can see and share the program's code. It is usually free to use. Shotcut says it is open source. Its page does not give more detail on the exact licence, so we say only that.

A free version of a paid product. The maker gives you a version with fewer tools and hopes some people will upgrade. DaVinci Resolve is like this.

Free with paid parts. You can start without paying, but some features, effects or sounds need a subscription. CapCut's terms say some features are free and others need payment.

None of these means every file you can click on is free to use in your work. The editor and the music inside it are separate questions.

DaVinci Resolve: what the free version offers

Blackmagic Design's page says DaVinci Resolve is available for Mac, Windows and Linux. About the free version, the page says it works with virtually all 8-bit video formats at up to 60 frames per second, and handles resolutions as high as Ultra HD (3840 x 2160). It also says the free version includes multi-user collaboration and HDR grading.

Studio is the paid upgrade. The page says it includes everything in the free version plus the DaVinci AI Neural Engine and extra tools such as more effects and noise reduction. It also lists 10-bit video up to 120 frames per second and resolutions beyond 4K.

What does that mean for you? Most phone videos are fine at these limits. Phones often record at 30 or 60 frames per second. If your camera records in a more advanced format than the free version supports, check Blackmagic's page before you start.

Resolve is a professional tool, so expect more to learn than in a phone app. We did not find its computer requirements on the page we opened. It links to a separate "Tech Specs" page, so check that page before you download, especially on an older computer.

CapCut: what the terms say about your videos, music and templates

CapCut is popular because it is quick. Its legal terms are worth reading, so here is what two of its pages say. The Terms of Service were last updated on 15 April 2026. The Materials License Agreement was last updated on 22 January 2026. Terms can change, so open them yourself.

Your videos. The terms say the company does not own your content. But you give it a non-exclusive, royalty-free, transferable, sub-licensable, perpetual and worldwide licence to use your content. That is a wide permission. Read it before you upload anything private or anything for a client.

Free and paid. The terms say some features are free and others need payment. Subscriptions renew automatically unless you cancel, and after you cancel you are moved to the free services.

Age. The general rule is 13 years or older. People under 18 need a parent's or guardian's consent. Some countries set different ages.

Music. The terms say no rights are licensed for sound recordings and musical works made available through the service. If you upload your own music, you must own it or have the rights.

Templates and effects. The Materials License says whether you can use a template or effect commercially depends on a mark. Items marked "Dual Use" can be used in certain commercial ways, such as promotional material for goods or services on e-commerce platforms. Items without that mark are for personal and non-commercial use. If a video mixes both kinds, you can use it only for personal and non-commercial purposes.

Sounds. The standard sound library is licensed for personal, non-commercial use. Using a sound to promote a brand or business needs separate rights. "Commercial Sounds" are offered separately to businesses, for use on the platforms named in the agreement.

The terms we read were in English. CapCut's features and rules may differ by country and app version, so we do not claim anything about watermarks. Check what the app shows you.

Shotcut: simple and open

Shotcut's own page says it supports resolutions up to 4K and hundreds of audio and video formats and codecs. It runs on Windows, Mac and Linux. It does not mention paid tiers on the page we read.

That makes it a simple choice if you want a desktop editor with no account story to worry about. It is a desktop program, so you install it on a computer. It does not remove the music question. Shotcut cannot give you rights to a song that you do not own.

How do I choose?

Your situationWorth a look
Quick clips for family and friendsCapCut, with its terms in mind
You want an open source desktop editorShotcut
You want professional colour and audio tools and have a capable computerDaVinci Resolve (free)
Videos for a paying client or your shop's advertsAny editor, but only with music and effects you have rights to

Ask three questions. What computer or phone do I have? Will money be involved? Where will I post? A video for your shop's WhatsApp status is different from one for a client's ad.

Common questions

Is it legal to use a popular song in my edited video?

Not automatically. Owning a copy of a song does not give you the right to use it in a video you share. Use music you made, or music whose licence clearly allows your use. The maker's terms, as with CapCut's, may restrict commercial use.

Can I sell videos I edit with a free editor?

The editor's licence is only part of the answer. Read its terms, and check every effect, template and sound inside the video. If a client pays you, you must have the rights to everything in it.

Should I download a cracked version of paid software?

No. Cracked software is illegal to use, and it is a common way for viruses to reach your computer. The free versions above are the safe route.

Which one is easiest?

That depends on you. Try a short clip in two editors and see which feels clear. Opinions differ, and we have not ranked them.

What to do next

  1. Write down your goal: for fun, for your shop, or for a client.
  2. Open each maker's page, read the terms that matter, and check the date at the top.
  3. Make a one-minute test video with your own clips and your own music, or music you have clear rights to.
  4. If your videos will help a shop, our post on a one-page marketing plan can help you decide what to say.

Your first edit will not be perfect. Every editor you admire began with a rough first cut, and you can learn this one clip at a time.
