item.title: From Diploma to Degree in Tanzania: What TCU Requires
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Can you join a bachelor's degree with an ordinary diploma? Here are the TCU minimum grades for 2026/27, the higher bars for health courses and how to check yours.
item.content:encoded:
You worked hard for your diploma, and maybe you have wondered whether it can still lead to a degree. For many people in Tanzania it can. There is an official route for it, and this post shows you the grades it asks for.

All figures below are as checked in November 2026, in the TCU guidebook for the 2026/27 admission year. Requirements change from year to year, so always read the current edition.

The short answer

Yes, you can apply for a bachelor's degree with an Ordinary Diploma (NTA Level 6). The Tanzania Commission for Universities (TCU) calls this "equivalent entry". The usual minimum is a Grade Point Average (GPA) of 3.0, plus enough O-Level passes.

  • At least four O-Level passes, each grade D or better.
  • A GPA of at least 3.0 for an Ordinary Diploma (NTA Level 6).
  • Diploma in Teacher Education: an average of B.
  • Health-related courses: an average of B or a GPA of 3.0, and at least five O-Level passes in non-religious subjects.
  • Nutrition and dietetics degrees: an average of B+ or a GPA of 3.5, and five O-Level passes.

Meeting the minimum does not promise a place. Each programme can ask for more, and places are limited.

What does "equivalent entry" mean?

TCU describes two kinds of entry to a degree. Direct entry is for people with Form Six or a foreign secondary certificate. Equivalent entry is for people who come through another recognised qualification, such as an Ordinary Diploma or the Foundation Certificate of the Open University of Tanzania.

So your diploma is not a second-class ticket. It is a named route in the official guidebook, with its own book. If you want to know where a diploma sits in the national ladder, read our post on NTA levels explained.

What are the minimum requirements for an Ordinary Diploma?

The guidebook for holders of an Ordinary Diploma has a table of general minimum entry requirements. For an Ordinary Diploma, FTC and equivalent qualifications, it asks for two things together.

First, O-Level. At least four passes (grade D and above) at O-Level, or NVA Level III with fewer than four O-Level passes, or equivalent foreign qualifications as established by NECTA or NACTVET.

Second, your diploma result. The table lists these by type of award:

Your awardMinimum in the guidebook
Ordinary Diploma (NTA Level 6)GPA of at least 3.0
Full Technician Certificate (FTC)Average of C (where A=5, B=4, C=3, D=2)
Diploma in Teacher EducationAverage of B
Health-related awards such as Clinical MedicineAverage of B
Unclassified diplomas and certificatesA Distinction
Classified non-NTA diplomasUpper Second Class

The guidebook also says that applicants who do not have at least 3.0 in the diploma or the Foundation Programme should not apply, because they do not meet the minimum.

Say your diploma GPA is 3.4 and you have five O-Level passes at D or better. That example is above both minimums in the general table. Say your GPA is 2.8. The guidebook advises you not to apply for a degree through this route.

What are the higher bars for health programmes?

Health courses have their own table, and it asks for more.

  • All health-related programmes: an appropriate Diploma or Advanced Diploma with an average of B or a GPA of at least 3.0, and at least five passes in non-religious subjects at O-Level.
  • Clinical Nutrition and Dietetics, and Food, Nutrition and Dietetics: a Diploma in Clinical Medicine, Agriculture, Nutrition, Environmental Health, Nursing or Midwifery with an average of B+ or a GPA of at least 3.5, plus five O-Level passes in non-religious subjects.

The word "appropriate" matters. Your diploma subject should fit the degree you want. Each institution's own page lists exactly which diplomas it accepts for each course.

How do I find my programme in the guidebook?

The guidebook is long, about 570 pages in the edition we read. Most of it is a list of institutions and their programmes. Here is a simple way to work.

  1. Open the guidebook for diploma holders, not the one for Form Six leavers. They are two different books.
  2. Read the general tables first (Table 1 for general courses, Table 2 for health).
  3. Use the search tool in your PDF reader. Type the name of the institution, then the programme.
  4. Read the whole row. Programmes can list the diplomas they accept, a minimum GPA or average, and sometimes a grade in a particular O-Level subject. One programme in the guidebook, for example, also asks for a "C" in Mathematics at O-Level.
  5. Note the programme's capacity, which is the number of places. Fewer places mean more competition.

Our post on how to read the TCU admission guidebook goes deeper into the tables.

What should I do if my GPA is just below 3.0?

This is a hard moment, and it is fine to feel disappointed. The guidebook is clear that applicants below the minimum are advised not to apply this way, so the honest answer is that this route is closed for now.

You still have options. Our post on what to do if you are not selected for university lists some. You can also ask your college whether a higher diploma or other course is open to you. Check that anything you pay for is at a registered institution first.

How do I apply?

TCU's undergraduate admissions page says you apply directly to the institution you choose. Each institution runs its own admission and announces its own successful applicants. The guidebook adds three useful rules:

  • Make sure the names and index numbers in your application match those on your exam records.
  • Questions about your application go to the institution you applied to.
  • If you are admitted to more than one institution, you must confirm the one you prefer.

Common questions

Is a GPA of 3.0 enough to be admitted?

It is the minimum to be eligible. It is not a guarantee. The programme may ask for more, and the number of applicants can be higher than the number of places.

What if I have fewer than four O-Level passes?

The table gives one other option: NVA Level III for those with fewer than four O-Level passes. Equivalent foreign qualifications are also listed. Ask your institution or NACTVET which applies to you.

Do these numbers stay the same every year?

Not always. That is why we say "as checked in November 2026". Read the guidebook for the year you want to apply.

Can I go from diploma to degree without Form Six?

The guidebook lists the diploma as its own route. Whether your own file qualifies depends on your O-Level passes and your diploma result, so check the table against your certificates.

What to do next

  1. Find your diploma result (GPA or average) and your O-Level results, and put them side by side with Table 1 or Table 2.
  2. Download the current guidebook for diploma holders from the TCU website.
  3. Make a short list of programmes and read each row in full.
  4. Check each institution's website for its application dates and portal.

You already finished one hard step. Taking the next one carefully is a good way to keep going.

Sources and further reading

  • Admission Guidebook for Holders of Ordinary Diploma or Equivalent Qualifications 2026/2027, Tanzania Commission for Universities
  • Undergraduate admissions, Tanzania Commission for Universities
  • Tanzania Qualifications Framework, Ministry of Education, Science and Technology

item.title: From Tennis for Two to PlayStation: A Short History of Games
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: Where video games came from, why there is no single first game, and how lab experiments became arcades, home consoles, Nintendo and PlayStation.
item.content:encoded:
Many of us remember the first time we shared a screen with a brother, a cousin or a friend. One person held the controller while the others shouted advice. That small joy has a long history, and it began with people who simply liked to tinker.

This post tells that story in short, using museum sources. It also answers a question people search all the time: what was the first video game?

The short answer: there is no single first video game

The answer depends on what you call a video game. If a game needs a screen, the answer is different from one that needs a computer or a home console. Museums list several early candidates, and they do not all agree on every year.

  • 1940: Nimatron, a machine that played the game Nim.
  • 1950: Bertie the Brain, a machine that played tic-tac-toe.
  • 1958: Tennis for Two, shown on an oscilloscope.
  • The early 1960s: Spacewar!, on a computer at MIT.
  • 1972: the Magnavox Odyssey, the first home game system, and Pong in arcades.
  • 1983 to 1989: Nintendo's home and handheld consoles.
  • 1994: the first PlayStation, launched in Japan.

What came before screens? Machines that played games (1940 to 1958)

In 1940, Westinghouse built a machine called Nimatron for the World's Fair. It was an electro-mechanical machine that played Nim, a simple game of taking turns to remove objects. The Strong National Museum of Play lists it as one early answer to the "first game" question.

In 1950, a custom-built machine called Bertie the Brain played tic-tac-toe against visitors at the Canadian National Exposition.

In 1958, scientists at Brookhaven National Laboratory made a tennis game for an oscilloscope, a screen that normally shows electric signals. It was called Tennis for Two, and it used custom controllers. It was shown at a public open house, and the Strong museum says an improved version followed the next year.

Think about that for a moment. Ordinary visitors to a science open day could play a simple tennis game made by scientists.

Why do the dates differ between sources?

Sources count different things. One may date a game from the day it was first shown. Another may use the day it was finished, or the day people could buy it. Tennis for Two is a good example. The Strong museum says it was shown at a public open house in 1958, and that an improved version followed the next year. Both dates tell a true part of the story.

The same care applies to the word "first". A machine that plays a game, a game on a screen, a game on a shared computer, a game in a bar and a game in your living room are all different firsts. When you read a claim that something was "the first video game", ask which of these it means.

Spacewar! and the campus years: the early 1960s

Next came computers at universities. The Strong museum says Spacewar! was made in 1963 by MIT students led by Steve Russell. Two players flew dueling spaceships on a digital computer, and the game spread to other computer centres.

The Computer History Museum says Spacewar! "came on the scene in 1961". The two museums give different years, so the safe way to say it is the early 1960s. The Computer History Museum also says it helped spark interest in programming on college campuses.

Games and computing grew up side by side.

Arcades and the first home consoles (1971 to 1972)

Around 1971, Nolan Bushnell and Nutting Associates released Computer Space, an arcade game where two ships try to destroy each other in outer space. The Strong museum says its controls were clumsy and it did not sell well.

In 1972, the Magnavox Odyssey arrived. The Strong museum calls it the first home video game system, an invention of Ralph Baer. It used analogue circuits. The Computer History Museum says Baer had built a prototype called the Brown Box in 1966.

Also in 1972, Atari's Pong brought video games to the public in a big way. The Computer History Museum says Allan Alcorn built the first prototype for Nolan Bushnell, and it was put in a bar in Sunnyvale, California, in 1972. It was so popular that it broke after it got jammed with coins.

We did not find a source that settles who borrowed ideas from whom between the Odyssey and Pong, so we leave that question alone.

The Computer History Museum calls the Atari 2600 "the most successful console of the 1970s and early 1980s". It names Pitfall! and Adventure among the games made for it.

Nintendo and the home console boom (1983 to 1989)

Nintendo's own history page gives these years:

  • 1983: the Family Computer System launched. Outside Japan it is known as the Nintendo Entertainment System.
  • 1985: Super Mario Bros. went on sale for that system.
  • 1989: the Game Boy handheld launched.

That page lists years only, not exact dates. The Game Boy was a handheld, so the game came with the player. Home consoles and handhelds are two different ways of playing, and Nintendo's page shows both in this short span of years.

PlayStation and the next step (1994 onward)

Sony's PlayStation site says its story starts when the original PlayStation launched in Japan in 1994. The racing series Gran Turismo began on that console in 1997, and the PlayStation 5 launched in 2020.

We have not source-checked other later parts of the story, such as phones, other console makers or sales numbers, so we leave them out. This post stops where our sources stop. For readers who want to continue, the museum pages in the list below are a good next step, and the history of later years is a fine topic for a future article.

Can you play old games today?

Some old games come back as official re-releases and collections from the companies that own them. If you want to try one, use the official store of the console or a trusted app store. Do not download copies from unknown sites. Those are often illegal, and they can carry harmful software.

If you pick a game for a young player, check its age label first. Our guide to game age ratings and parental controls explains how.

Why does this history matter?

It shows that games came from curiosity. Scientists, students and engineers tried things for the pleasure of seeing them work. A simple idea, such as two paddles and a ball, grew into a world industry over a few decades. Every big change started with someone who made something small and let other people try it.

Common questions

What was the first video game?

There is no single answer. The Strong National Museum of Play lists Nimatron (1940), Bertie the Brain (1950), Tennis for Two (1958), Spacewar! (early 1960s), the Odyssey and Pong (1972) as candidates. Your answer depends on your definition.

Was Pong the first video game?

Pong was not the first game. The Strong museum says it became a widespread hit and brought video games to the public for the first time. Earlier games existed in labs and universities.

Which was the first home console?

The Strong museum names the Magnavox Odyssey of 1972 as the first home video game system.

When did PlayStation start?

Sony says the original PlayStation launched in Japan in 1994.

What to do next

  1. Read the Strong museum's article on the first video game and form your own view.
  2. Ask an older relative which game they played first, and listen to the story.
  3. If you like making things, look for a free beginner course on programming. Early game makers learned by trying.
  4. Share this page with someone who loves games.

Every big industry starts small. A tennis game on an oscilloscope was once all there was.

Sources and further reading

  • What was the first video game?, The Strong National Museum of Play
  • Computers and games: a love story, Computer History Museum
  • Nintendo history, Nintendo Co., Ltd.
  • About PlayStation, Sony Interactive Entertainment

item.title: Game Age Ratings Explained: ESRB, PEGI and Parental Controls
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: What ESRB, PEGI and the ratings on Google Play mean, what they leave out, and how to set limits on a phone or console, with a talk-first plan for parents.
item.content:encoded:
Your child asks to install a new game, and you want to say yes. You also want to know what is inside it. Many parents and guardians feel the same worry, because games arrive on phones with very little explanation.

This guide explains the age labels in plain words, shows what you will see on Google Play, and gives the steps to set limits. As checked in November 2026, these are the facts on the official pages listed at the end.

The short answer

An age rating tells you what kind of content a game has, such as violence or strong language. It is advice for adults, and it does not tell you if the game is good, safe or cheap. Read the label, then look at the extras that ratings do not cover: chat, spending and random items.

  • ESRB and PEGI are two well-known rating systems. Each uses an age label and short notes about content.
  • On Google Play, many countries without their own rating body see a generic set of labels: 3+, 7+, 12+, 16+ and 18+.
  • Ratings are guidance. We did not find any Tanzanian rule that makes these labels compulsory, so treat them as advice, not law.
  • You can turn on content limits on Google Play with a PIN your child does not know.
  • The best tool is still a talk with your child, before you lock anything.

What do ESRB ratings mean?

The ESRB is the Entertainment Software Rating Board. It uses five main labels:

LabelWhat the ESRB says
EveryoneContent is generally suitable for all ages
Everyone 10+Content is generally suitable for ages 10 and up
TeenContent is generally suitable for ages 13 and up
Mature 17+Content is generally suitable for ages 17 and up
Adults Only 18+Content is suitable only for adults aged 18 and up

Next to the label you may see content descriptors. These are short notes such as Blood, Violence, Language or Gambling Themes. They explain why the game got its rating.

The ESRB also shows "interactive elements". These tell you about online features: In-Game Purchases, Includes Random Items, Users Interact and Shares Location. The ESRB says these do not change the age rating. That matters, and we come back to it below.

What do PEGI ratings mean?

PEGI is another well-known system. It has five age labels: 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18. In short:

  • PEGI 3: suitable for everyone. Very mild, comic violence is allowed.
  • PEGI 7: may have scenes or sounds that could frighten younger children. Violence is very mild or not realistic.
  • PEGI 12: more graphic violence toward fantasy characters, or non-realistic violence toward human-like characters. Mild swearing and sexual hints may appear.
  • PEGI 16: violence or sexual activity can look like real life. Stronger language, and tobacco, alcohol or illegal drugs, may appear.
  • PEGI 18: the most serious content, including gross violence, simulated gambling and explicit sexual activity.

PEGI also uses content symbols, such as violence, bad language and fear. Its page says the age labels are about suitability by content and risks, and it does not say anything about how hard a game is.

PEGI has added more notes about online risks. These include in-game purchases, paid random items and chat that cannot be blocked or muted. Its page says some new rules apply to games submitted since June 2026, for example a higher rating for paid random items. Older games may not follow those newer rules, so always read the label on the game you are looking at.

What will you see on Google Play in Tanzania?

Most families here meet games through the Google Play Store on an Android phone. Google Play uses a system called IARC, which works with rating bodies around the world. The developer answers a questionnaire, and the rating comes from the answers.

Google's help page says that in countries without a rating body of their own, Play shows generic IARC ratings. The labels are Rated for 3+, 7+, 12+, 16+ and 18+. We could not confirm from Google's page which exact label Tanzania sees, so check the live listing on your own phone. The Play Store also shows ratings by the viewer's country, so a friend abroad may see a different label for the same game.

Please remember that none of this is a Tanzanian law on games. It is a safety guide from companies and rating groups. We did not find an official Tanzanian source that sets age ratings for games, so we do not claim one exists.

If you name a game in a family talk, open its page and read the label yourself. A friend's memory of a game is not a rating.

What does a rating not tell you?

A rating mostly describes content. It does not tell you about three things that often worry parents more.

  1. Chat with strangers. The ESRB label "Users Interact" says players can meet user-made content and talk to each other. A game rated for young children can still have chat.
  2. Spending. "In-Game Purchases" means you can buy things with real money. A game can be free to install and still ask for money again and again.
  3. Random items. "Includes Random Items" means you pay without knowing what you will get. We explain this in our guide on loot boxes and in-game purchases.

So the label is the first step, not the last. Look at the full listing, read recent reviews, and ask what the game lets your child do with other players.

How do you set limits on a phone, console or PC?

On an Android phone with Google Play

Google's help page gives these steps for a family member who manages their own account:

  1. Open the Google Play app and tap the profile icon at the top right.
  2. Tap Settings, then Family, then Content restrictions.
  3. Tap Go to Parental controls, then set up a parental controls PIN.
  4. Choose a PIN your child does not know.
  5. Select the types of content you want to filter, then choose how to limit access.

If your child has an account managed with the Family Link app, open Family Link, pick your child, tap Controls, then Google Play, and choose what to filter.

Know what these settings cannot do, as Google explains:

  • They work only on the device where you set them. Repeat the steps on every phone or tablet your child uses.
  • Restricted apps can still show in search or open through a direct link.
  • Games installed before you set the limit stay on the phone. Family Link can block them on a child's device.
  • Menus change, and some options are not offered in every country. If a step looks different, search Google Play Help for the current page.

On consoles and PCs

Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo and Windows each have their own family tools, and the menus change often. We did not open every platform page, so we do not give menu steps here. The ESRB Family Gaming Guide is a good place to start. It lists parental controls and child accounts, and it advises giving each child their own account so that limits on ratings, schedules, contacts and purchases can be set for that child. Then open the support page of your console maker and follow its current steps.

Talk with your child before you lock things

A lock without a conversation can feel like a punishment. A child who feels trusted is more likely to come to you when something goes wrong, such as a rude message or a surprise charge.

Here is a plain way to start. Sit beside your child and ask to see the game. Ask who they play with. Ask what the game lets them buy. Then agree some house rules together, such as when the phone is put away and what you will say yes to without asking.

The ESRB guide suggests the same idea: agree on limits for screen time, spending and online chat, and set rules that match each child's age. For children under about five it suggests adult supervision. For the middle years it suggests checking ratings and contacts. For teenagers it suggests open talk, with rules that loosen as they show they can handle more.

You do not need to be a gamer to do this. You only need to be interested.

Common questions

Is an ESRB or PEGI label a law in Tanzania?

We did not find a Tanzanian rule that makes these labels compulsory. They are guidance from rating bodies. The Play Store shows ratings by country, and the generic labels are advice for adults.

Does a low rating mean a game is safe?

No. A rating covers content. It does not cover chat, spending or random items. A game rated for young children can still let players talk or buy things.

Can my child get around Google Play limits?

Content restrictions are not perfect. Google says restricted apps can still appear in search or open from a link, and old installs stay. A PIN your child does not know helps, and so does talking.

What if I forget my parental controls PIN?

Google's page says you can clear the storage of the Play Store app to reset the PIN and the restrictions. This also removes your settings, so write them down first.

What to do next

  1. Open your child's most used game on Google Play and read its rating, its reviews and its purchase notes.
  2. Set a Content restrictions PIN on each device your child uses, and keep the PIN to yourself.
  3. Read the ESRB Family Gaming Guide and pick two house rules to try this week.
  4. Sit with your child for ten minutes while they play, and ask them to show you their favourite part.

Small steps count. A calm talk tonight is worth more than a perfect setting you never explain.

Sources and further reading

  • Ratings Guide, Entertainment Software Rating Board (ESRB)
  • What do the labels mean, PEGI
  • Content ratings on Google Play, Google Play Console Help
  • Set up parental controls on Google Play, Google Play Help
  • Family Gaming Guide, ESRB

item.title: Healthy Gaming Habits: How to Tell When Play Becomes a Problem
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: What the World Health Organization says about gaming disorder, what healthy play looks like, and fair family rules, with when to ask a health professional.
item.content:encoded:
If you are a parent or guardian, you may feel a quiet worry when your child plays for hours. You may also feel guilty for feeling it. If you are a young person, you may feel that everyone is judging something you simply enjoy. Both feelings are normal, and neither one makes anyone a bad person.

This post sets out what the World Health Organization (WHO) actually says, what healthy play can look like, and how a family can agree on fair rules. It is general information, not medical advice. For any real concern, please talk to a qualified health professional.

The short answer

There is no magic number of hours that is "too much". WHO says that gaming disorder affects only a small share of people who play, so most players are not affected. What matters more is whether play is crowding out the rest of life.

  • WHO describes gaming disorder by three features: impaired control, gaming taking priority over other activities, and continuing despite harm.
  • It would normally be clear for at least 12 months.
  • ESRB and a paediatric group both advise family rules made together, not hours dictated from above.
  • Sleep, school, food, friends and movement are the things to protect.
  • A health professional, not a website, should decide whether something is a problem.

What the World Health Organization says

WHO's page on gaming disorder explains how it appears in the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11). We read it in November 2026. It describes gaming disorder as a pattern of gaming behaviour. It lists three features:

  1. Impaired control over gaming.
  2. Increasing priority given to gaming over other activities, over other activities.
  3. Continuing or increasing gaming even when negative consequences appear.

WHO also says the pattern must be severe enough to significantly impair a person's functioning. It adds that this would normally have been clear for at least 12 months.

Then comes the most important sentence for worried families. WHO says gaming disorder affects only a small proportion of people who play digital or video games. Most people who play are not affected.

WHO also gives advice to players themselves. It suggests that people who game should watch how much time they spend on it, especially when it takes over from other daily activities. They should also notice any change in their physical or mental health, or in their social life, that could be linked to gaming.

This page is a description of what WHO says. It is not a test you can use at home. Only a trained professional can say whether someone has a disorder.

What healthy play looks like day to day

Games can be fun, social and creative. Many young people play to be with friends. Some learn teamwork, patience and quick thinking. Healthy play usually sits comfortably beside everything else in a person's day.

Here are signs that play is fitting in well:

  • Homework and school duties get done.
  • Meals, sleep and family time still happen.
  • The player can stop when asked, perhaps after a short grumble.
  • There is still time for friends outside games, and for moving the body.
  • The player seems generally well in mood and health.

The ESRB, which rates games in North America, says on its family guide that it gives no fixed number of hours. It suggests asking whether gaming gets in the way of other activities or responsibilities.

WHO's physical activity page says any amount of physical activity is better than none, and that people of every age should limit time spent sitting. It gives no screen-time limit for children, so we do not invent one here. A football game with neighbours, a walk to the shop or helping at home all count as movement.

Signs to watch, and what they do not prove

If you are worried, it helps to watch the pattern over time, not one bad evening. Using WHO's own words as a guide, you might notice:

  • Your child cannot seem to cut down, even when they want to.
  • Games keep winning over schoolwork, meals, sleep or friends.
  • Play continues even after real trouble, such as falling grades or constant arguments.
  • Changes in mood, health or friendships that seem linked to gaming.

None of these signs proves a disorder. A child may play late during a school holiday. A teenager may be upset about something else that has nothing to do with games. Heavy play can sometimes be a way to cope with stress, loneliness or bullying, and the real issue may lie elsewhere.

So please do not label your child, and do not label yourself. Describe what you see, stay curious, and ask for help if the worry stays. Avoid casual words such as "addict". WHO uses careful wording, and a harsh label can make a young person stop talking to you.

Fair family rules that children accept

Rules work better when children help make them. Here are ideas drawn from the ESRB and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), which publishes a family media plan.

  1. Start with a calm talk. The ESRB suggests a conversation without judgement that accepts games are part of your child's life. Ask what they enjoy about their favourite game.
  2. Agree on simple rules together. An example from the ESRB is play after homework is finished, or devices put away at dinner.
  3. Use screen-free zones. The AAP names the dinner table, homework time and bedtime as times to keep screens away. It says this supports family connection, learning and sleep.
  4. Allow logical stopping points. Some games only save at certain places, and leaving an online match can let teammates down. The ESRB suggests giving a few extra minutes, such as "five more minutes", to respect your child's hobby and friendships.
  5. Make room for other things. The AAP suggests reading, outdoor play, family games and hobbies, so that screens do not crowd out other experiences.
  6. Choose content with care. Check age ratings before a game is installed. See our post on game age ratings and parental controls.
  7. Review the rules. The ESRB says to revisit rules as children grow. The AAP suggests reviewing at the start of a school year or during holidays.

Parental controls on devices can help too. The ESRB says they can manage who your child plays with, how much they can spend, and when and for how long they play. It calls them a backup to house rules, not a replacement for talking.

Money is part of healthy play as well. If your child buys items in a game, read our post on loot boxes and in-game purchases.

One more thing about rules. Try to follow them yourself. If the family rule is no phones at dinner, that includes adults. Children notice, and they respond to fairness.

When to ask for help

Consider talking to a doctor, a clinical psychologist or another qualified health professional if:

  • the worry has lasted and does not ease with kind, clear family rules;
  • sleep, school, health or relationships are clearly suffering;
  • your child seems very low, anxious or withdrawn;
  • you are unsure what is happening and want a professional opinion.

You do not have to wait for a perfect moment. Asking early is not an overreaction. Start with a local clinic or hospital, or with a school counsellor if your child's school has one. We cannot name a specific service for every area, so please ask a local health worker where to go.

If you are a young person reading this and feel your gaming is hard to control, you are not weak. Tell someone you trust, such as a parent, an older relative or a teacher, and ask them to help you find a health professional.

Common questions

How many hours of gaming is too many?

Neither WHO nor the ESRB gives a number on the pages we read. The ESRB suggests asking whether play gets in the way of other activities. If sleep, school, meals or friendships are suffering, it is time for a calm talk.

Does my child have gaming disorder if they play every day?

Not necessarily. WHO says most people who play games are not affected. Only a professional can judge. Daily play that fits well with school, family and sleep is not the same as the pattern WHO describes.

Should I take the console or phone away?

Sudden punishment often leads to hiding and arguments. The ESRB recommends talking first, building rules together and allowing sensible stopping points. If you do set a limit, explain why and say when you will review it.

Are games always bad for children?

No. Games can be a way to enjoy time with friends and to learn. The question is balance and content. Check the age rating and keep other parts of life going.

What to do next

  1. Choose a calm time and ask your child what they like about their games. Listen first.
  2. Write two or three family rules together, such as screens off at dinner and at bedtime, and review them in a few weeks.
  3. Add something active or social that the whole family can enjoy.
  4. If the worry continues, speak with a qualified health professional.

Caring about how your child plays is a form of love. Keep the door open, stay kind, and remember that you are on the same side.

Sources and further reading

  • Gaming disorder (ICD-11 frequently asked questions), World Health Organization
  • Managing screen time, Family Gaming Guide, ESRB
  • How to make a family media use plan, HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics
  • Physical activity fact sheet, World Health Organization

item.title: How a New Online Seller Can Earn Customer Trust in Tanzania
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: No reviews yet? Learn simple, honest habits that help strangers trust a new online shop in Tanzania, from clear photos to receipts and fast replies.
item.content:encoded:
Starting a shop with no reviews and no followers can feel lonely. You post a good product and nobody replies. That silence is normal. Strangers do not know you yet, and many have been cheated before, so they hold back.

You cannot make people trust you in one day. You can give them many small reasons to relax. This post lists those reasons, one by one, using advice from official pages and from the platforms sellers use.

The short answer

Trust grows from small habits that you repeat every day. Show who you are, describe your goods honestly, let buyers feel safe about payment and delivery, give receipts, and answer quickly and fairly. None of this costs much. No habit here guarantees sales, but each one removes a reason for a buyer to say no.

  • Put your name, place and opening hours where buyers can see them.
  • Use your own photos and say the real size, colour and price.
  • Offer payment after the buyer has seen the item, where you can.
  • Give a receipt and keep a record of every sale.
  • Reply fast, stay calm with complaints, and ask for feedback politely.

Why buyers are careful

Online fraud is a daily worry in Tanzania. The Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority (TCRA) runs public campaigns to warn people about scam messages and about sending money to strangers. As checked in November 2026, it advises people not to send money from their phone to someone they do not know, and to check the message and the number before paying.

So when a stranger looks at your shop, they are not judging you. They are protecting their money. Think of each habit below as an answer to a question the buyer is asking in their head: "Is this person real? Is this item real? Will I be safe?"

Show who you are

A shop with no face is hard to trust. Give buyers one place where they can learn the basics.

If you use WhatsApp Business, fill in the business profile. WhatsApp's own page for the Business app says a business profile can give helpful information for your customers in one place, and that this helps you make a good first impression. Add your shop name, what you sell, your area (for example Kariakoo, Mwenge or Kisutu), and your opening hours.

On other apps, do the same in the bio. Use the same name and the same phone number everywhere. If your name changes from page to page, buyers wonder why.

Use a clear profile picture. A photo of your real shelf or your real products works better than a stock picture or a copied one.

Does a registered business help?

The Business Registrations and Licensing Agency (BRELA) lists benefits of holding a business licence on its website. One of them, in Swahili, is "kuaminika kwa wateja", which means being trusted by customers. Others are recognition by banks and a better chance of getting loans.

We did not find a page saying that a small seller on social media must be registered before selling. Rules depend on your kind of business and where you work, so check the BRELA and TRA pages for your own case. Our guide to registering a small business in Tanzania explains the steps. If you register, you can say so in your profile. Do not claim a licence you do not hold.

Say exactly what you sell

Most disputes begin with a gap between what the buyer imagined and what arrived. Close that gap before the sale.

  • Take photos in daylight, from more than one side. Show the real item, not a picture from a catalogue.
  • Write the size, colour, material and condition. If the item is used, say so and show any scratch or mark.
  • State the price in TSh, and say what it includes. If delivery costs extra, give that price too.
  • Say how long delivery takes in your area, and be honest. Two days promised and four days delivered hurts more than four days promised and four delivered.
  • If you do not have an item in stock, say so.

Never use another seller's pictures and never claim a brand you do not sell. A copied photo is easy to spot and quickly ends the conversation.

Let buyers feel safe about payment and delivery

The biggest fear is paying first and receiving nothing. Jiji, the online marketplace, tells its buyers to check a seller's feedback, to avoid paying upfront, to look at the item before paying, and to meet sellers face to face in a public place. That list tells you what careful buyers will want from you.

You can meet them halfway:

  1. Offer pay after inspection. Jiji's advice to sellers is not to ask for payment upfront, because buyers are wary of sending money before they see the item. It suggests delivery services that let buyers pay after they inspect the product.
  2. Meet in a public place when the buyer collects the item, such as a busy shop front or a well-known bus stop.
  3. Be clear about mobile money. Give the number and the registered name, and let the buyer see that the name matches. Never ask a buyer to send "a small deposit to hold the item" unless you are ready to explain it and return it if they change their mind.
  4. Do not rush the buyer. Pressure ("pay now, only one left") looks like the scam messages people already know.

If you sell items that cost a lot, you can expect more questions. That is fine. Answer each one patiently.

Protect yourself too

Trust runs both ways. Fake payment messages are a risk for sellers. Check that the money has really arrived in your account before you hand over the goods, and do not rely on a screenshot or a message alone. TCRA advises people to check the message and the number, and to call their provider on 100 if they are unsure.

Give receipts and keep records

A receipt tells the buyer that you are a real business that expects to be found again. It also protects you when someone says "I never got it".

The Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA) prints a slogan on its website: "Whenever you sell, issue receipt. Whenever you buy, demand receipt." As checked in November 2026, TRA says that a person who supplies goods or services and has an annual turnover assessed at TSh 11 million or more must use an electronic fiscal device (EFD) to issue fiscal receipts. A very small seller may be below that line, but you may still give a simple receipt.

A simple receipt can show:

  • your shop name and phone number,
  • the date,
  • what was sold, the quantity and the price,
  • how it was paid,
  • a line saying how to reach you if there is a problem.

Keep a copy. A notebook or a photo of each receipt on your phone is enough to start. Records also help you see which items sell and which come back. Ask TRA or a tax adviser what applies to your turnover, because tax rules can change.

Reply fast and handle complaints fairly

Speed shows respect. Jiji tells sellers not to make buyers wait too long for a reply. If you cannot answer at once, set a short message such as "Thank you, I will reply by 6 pm." Then do it.

When something goes wrong:

  1. Listen to the whole complaint before you answer.
  2. Say sorry if it is your fault, in one plain sentence.
  3. Offer a fix you can really deliver: a replacement, an exchange, or a refund.
  4. Do it quickly and tell the buyer when it is done.

Tanzanian consumer law may give buyers rights on returns and refunds. We could not confirm the details for this post, so check the Fair Competition Commission, which handles consumer protection, for the current rules. Whatever the law says, a clear return rule written in your profile (for example, "Tell me within 24 hours if the item is damaged") is easier on everyone.

Asking for feedback

Jiji says that inviting buyers to share their experience after a sale makes it more likely that new buyers will choose you, because your rating depends on the feedback you get. Ask once, politely, after the item has arrived. Never write reviews for yourself and never pay for fake ones. Our post on asking customers for reviews honestly has wording you can use, and the one on fake followers and "guaranteed sales" offers explains why shortcuts hurt.

Common questions

How long does it take to build trust?

There is no fixed time. It depends on your product, your area and how often you sell. Expect the first sales to come mostly from people who already know you or who ask questions first and see that you answer well.

Should I ask for money before I deliver?

Many buyers do not like this, and Jiji advises sellers against it. Where you can, let the buyer pay after seeing the item. If you must take a deposit, for example for something made to order, explain why in writing and give a receipt.

Do I need a website to be trusted?

No. A tidy WhatsApp Business profile or social page with real photos, a phone number and clear prices is a fine start. A website can come later.

What if a buyer leaves an unfair complaint?

Stay polite, give the facts once, and offer to fix what is truly wrong. Other buyers read how you respond, and a calm answer says a lot about you.

What to do next

  1. Write your shop profile today: name, products, area, hours and phone number. Use the same text on every page.
  2. Retake photos of your five best items in daylight and write honest descriptions.
  3. Print or write a simple receipt format and use it for the next sale.
  4. Write your return and delivery rules in two or three lines and pin them where buyers can see them.

Every kept promise is a small brick, and a shop with no name today can have one in a year. Start with the next order.

If you are still choosing what to sell, see low-cost ways to start an online business in Tanzania.

Sources and further reading

  • WhatsApp Business app, WhatsApp (Meta)
  • Business licence services and benefits, BRELA
  • How to stay safe when buying, Jiji Tanzania
  • Advice for sellers, Jiji Tanzania
  • EFD and VFD suppliers and who must use them, Tanzania Revenue Authority
  • TCRA launches campaign to curb online fraud, Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority

item.title: How Do AI Chatbots Work? A Plain-Words Explanation
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: A chatbot answers by guessing the next piece of a sentence, again and again. See what that means, why it can be wrong, and what it cannot do.
item.content:encoded:
You type a question into a chatbot and, a few seconds later, you get a neat answer. It feels like talking to someone clever. You may wonder how a machine can do this, and whether you can trust it. The idea behind it is simpler than most people think, and understanding it will help you use these tools with confidence.

The short answer

An AI chatbot is built on a language model. A language model estimates which word, or piece of a word, is likely to come next, given the text so far. The chatbot repeats that step many times and builds an answer one piece at a time.

  • It predicts text. It does not look up one true answer in a book.
  • It learned patterns from a very large amount of writing during training.
  • That is why it sounds fluent, and also why it can be wrong and still sound sure.
  • It does not have feelings, and it does not know you.
  • You still need to check what it tells you.

The phone keyboard idea: guessing the next word

Here is an analogy. It is only an analogy, because a chatbot is far more powerful than your phone keyboard. When you type "Habari za" on your phone, the keyboard may suggest "asubuhi" or "leo". It does this because those words often follow. It is guessing the next word from what you typed.

A language model does something like this, on a much bigger scale. Google's machine learning course describes a language model as a system that estimates how likely a token, or a series of tokens, is to appear in a longer series. A token is the smallest unit the model works with. It can be a whole word, part of a word or a single character. Google says most modern models use word pieces, and for English one token is about four characters, or roughly three-quarters of a word.

Google gives an example. Take the sentence "When I hear rain on my roof, I ___ in my kitchen." A model might give "cook soup" a probability of 9.4% and "warm up a kettle" 5.2%. A program then picks one, either the most likely option or a random choice from the likely ones. That small step is the heart of it.

What happens between pressing send and seeing a reply?

Here is a simple version of the steps. Real systems have more parts, but this shows the idea.

  1. You type your question and press send.
  2. Your text is cut into tokens.
  3. The model looks at the tokens and gives a probability to each possible next token.
  4. One token is chosen and added to the text.
  5. The model looks at the text again, including the new token, and chooses the next one.
  6. This repeats until the answer is complete, and the words appear on your screen.

Because a chatbot works one piece at a time, it is writing as it goes. It is not copying a finished answer from a hidden shelf.

What does context do?

Context means the words around the spot you want to guess. Google's page uses the word "orange". With the words around it, the model can tell whether you mean the fruit or the colour. Older, simpler methods looked at only a couple of words before the gap and made many mistakes. Google says large language models can look at the whole context at once, which is one reason they handle long questions better.

This is also why a clear question gets a better answer. The more useful words you give, the better the guess. Our post on how to write a good AI prompt shows how.

Training: learning patterns from a very large amount of text

Before anyone uses a chatbot, the model goes through training. In training, the model is shown a great deal of written text and learns which patterns of words tend to appear together. Think of a student who reads thousands of books and starts to notice how sentences usually go. Again, this is an analogy. A model does not "understand" a book the way you do.

We are not going to state how much text any company used, because those figures come from the companies and we cannot check them. The main point is enough: the chatbot learned patterns of language from its training material, and it uses those patterns to guess what comes next.

Two results follow:

  • It can write fluent, well-formed sentences on many topics.
  • What it "knows" is limited by what it was trained on. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, says on its help page that a model may not have the most up-to-date training data and can be confused about current events. Some chatbots can also search the web, which helps, but their summary can still leave things out.

Why can a chatbot sound sure and still be wrong?

Because it is built to produce likely text, not to check facts. A sentence can be likely and false at the same time.

The companies say so themselves. Anthropic's help page says its model can give incorrect or misleading answers, which it calls "hallucinating", and that it may write quotes that sound authoritative but are not grounded in fact. It advises people not to treat the chatbot as their only source of truth. Google's help page for Gemini says the tool may sometimes give inaccurate information and that you should double-check its answers, including when it describes how it works.

This matters most for:

  • Names, dates, prices and numbers.
  • Quotes and book or study titles.
  • Medical, legal and money questions.
  • School and exam facts, such as fees, cut-offs and rules.

For those, always check an official source. In Tanzania that could be the TCU, NECTA or HESLB website, or the page of the office involved.

Myth or fact?

MythFact
"The chatbot looks up the right answer."It predicts likely text. Some tools add a web search, but the writing is still a guess.
"If it sounds confident, it is right."Confidence in the wording says nothing about accuracy.
"It thinks and feels like a person."It produces text from patterns. It has no feelings.
"It knows everything up to today."Training material has a cut-off date, and it may be out of date.
"One good answer means all answers are good."Quality changes from question to question. Check each one.

What can a chatbot not do?

  • It cannot feel, care or hold a real opinion. If it says "I am happy to help," that is a way of writing, not a feeling.
  • It cannot be trusted as your only source for facts that matter.
  • It cannot know your private situation unless you tell it. If you tell it, think first. Read what not to paste into AI chatbots before you share personal details.
  • It cannot replace a doctor, lawyer, teacher or adviser. Google's page says not to treat the answers as medical, legal, financial or other professional advice.

None of this means chatbots are useless. They can help you brainstorm, explain a hard idea in simpler words, check your spelling or draft an email you will then correct. See our list of AI tools for productivity for ideas. The skill is to use them as a helper and to stay in charge.

Common questions

Is a chatbot the same as a search engine?

No. A search engine finds pages that already exist. A chatbot writes new text by predicting words. Some chatbots now include a search step, and then it is worth opening the pages they cite, because the original page may include things the summary left out.

Why does the answer change when I ask again?

An application can choose among likely tokens instead of always taking the top one, as Google describes. So the same question can give different wording each time.

Does a chatbot understand what I say?

We avoid saying it understands, because we cannot show that. What we can say is that it handles the words you give it and produces a likely reply.

Can I use a chatbot for homework?

Use it to learn, not to hand in its words as yours. Check each fact in a reliable source and write the final work yourself. Your school or university may have its own rules, so follow them.

How do I check an answer?

Look for the claim in an official or trusted source, check the date, and be most careful with numbers and quotes. If you cannot confirm it, do not repeat it.

What to do next

  1. Try the keyboard idea: type half a sentence and see what your phone suggests. It shows how guessing works.
  2. Ask a chatbot a question you already know the answer to, and see where it is right and where it is wrong.
  3. Next time you use one, pick one fact from the answer and confirm it in an official source.
  4. Learn to spot AI voice and video scams, because the same technology can be misused.

You do not need to be an engineer to use these tools well. You need curiosity and the habit of checking, and you already have both.

Sources and further reading

  • Introduction to large language models, Google for Developers
  • Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what's going on?, Anthropic
  • Gemini Apps Help: how Gemini works and its limits, Google

item.title: How Esports Works, and Where Africa and Tanzania Fit In
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: What esports is, how federations and organisers run tournaments, what is known about Africa and Tanzania, and why school and health come first.
item.content:encoded:
If you love games, you may have asked yourself a quiet question: can this lead anywhere? Many young Tanzanians ask it, and many parents ask it too. The honest answer has hope in it, and it also has limits.

This post explains how esports is organised, who runs it, and what we could confirm about Africa and Tanzania. Where we could not find facts, we say so. Dated facts below were checked in November 2026.

The short answer

Esports means organised, competitive video games, played by teams or single players in set events with rules and referees. It works like other sports in one way: there are organisers, federations, qualifiers and champions. It is also very hard to reach the top, and no result can be promised.

  • Esports has governing bodies, such as the International Esports Federation (IESF).
  • Even players on big club programmes must qualify on their own merit for each event, according to the Esports World Cup Foundation.
  • The eSports Federation of Tanzania was announced as a new IESF member on 17 March 2025.
  • We found very little public detail about Tanzanian players, teams or events, and we do not invent any.
  • School, health and sleep come first. Many popular esports games carry teen or adult ratings.

What is esports, and what is it not?

Esports is competition. Players or teams meet in a game, under the same rules, and a winner is decided. Some events are played in an arena and watched by fans. Many are played online.

It is not the same as playing for fun at home. Casual play is a good hobby, and it does not need to become a career. Esports is also not a quick way to earn money. We do not give income figures, because we cannot verify them, and we will not suggest that anyone can "go pro" by playing more hours.

This post does not cover betting, and we do not link to betting sites.

How do players and teams reach a tournament?

There is no single path, because each game and each organiser sets its own rules. What the sources we opened do show is this:

  1. Qualifiers come first. The Esports World Cup Foundation says that all clubs and athletes must seek to qualify on their own merits for each title. That is true even for clubs in its support programme. A club programme does not guarantee a place.
  2. National federations can send teams. The IESF says it works to give nations chances to compete through championships and programmes. Its first world championship was in 2009 with eight nations.
  3. Rules are set by each organiser. Age limits, entry rules and games change from one event to another. Read the official rules of the event you care about, and be careful with any page that asks for money to "guarantee" entry.

Say you are a student who plays a team game every evening. A sensible plan is to learn which organisers run events for that game, read their rules, and join only free or low-cost open events that you can verify. This is an example, not a promise of any result.

Please be careful with offers that look too good. Do not pay a stranger for a place in a tournament, and do not share your passwords with a "coach" or a "team" you have not checked.

Who runs esports? Federations and organisers

Two examples show the kinds of groups involved.

The International Esports Federation (IESF). Its own page says it is the global governing body for esports. It was founded in 2008 in Seoul, South Korea, and now lists its headquarters in Busan. It says it has more than 150 member nations, up from 50 in 2013 and 100 in 2017. It states that it aims to promote esports as a legitimate sport, set standards, and protect fair play.

The Esports World Cup Foundation. It runs the Esports World Cup and has a Club Support Program. Its news page says the programme helps multi-game esports clubs build lasting infrastructure, and that accepted clubs can receive large funding. The page also repeats that club members must still qualify on merit.

Besides these, game makers and private companies run their own leagues. We did not open pages for them, so we do not describe them.

What does the Africa scene look like?

Here our sources are narrower, and we want to be clear about what they cover.

The 2025 Africa Games Industry Report was published by KPMG with Maliyo Games. A report in ThisDay says Africa earned less than 1% of the 187 billion US dollars that the world games industry made in 2024. It also says the report counted 66 active studios and named barriers such as weak government support, limited funding and technical infrastructure, poor power supply and limited access to training.

Two points need care. First, this is about the games industry, meaning the businesses that make games. It is not a measure of esports. Second, we did not open the report itself, so we use only the figures from the news article, and we do not quote any esports or mobile share figures.

What does that mean for a young person? It suggests that the industry is young, and that power, internet and training are real obstacles. It also suggests there is room to grow. We cannot say more than that.

Tanzania: what is known and what is not

One fact is sourced. The news site Esports Advocate reported on 17 March 2025 that the IESF added five new member federations, and that the eSports Federation of Tanzania was one of them. That brought the total to 151 members. The report said the new members would take part in the IESF 2025 Season.

That is where our verified information ends. We found the IESF member page for Tanzania, but it has no description. We did not find a source about a Tanzanian national team, a national tournament, prize money or named players, so we say nothing about them.

If you want to know more, ask the federation or the IESF directly, and check any claim you read on social media against an official page. If you know of an event in your town, look at who runs it and what the rules say before you join.

Which games are involved, and are they right for you?

Many popular esports titles have teen or adult ratings. Before you or your child joins an event, check the game's age label on its official page. Our guide to game age ratings and parental controls explains how the labels work. We do not name particular games here, because we have not checked their ratings.

Also watch spending. Some games sell random items, and our guide to loot boxes and in-game purchases shows how to set limits on Google Play.

Common questions

Can I make a living from esports in Tanzania?

We cannot promise that. We found no verified figures for Tanzania, and reaching the top of any competitive field is difficult. Treat esports as something to enjoy and learn from, while you keep studying.

Is there a national esports federation in Tanzania?

The IESF added the eSports Federation of Tanzania as a member, as reported on 17 March 2025. We could not find a description of its work, so ask it directly for details.

Do I need an expensive computer?

That depends on the game. We did not check hardware needs, so look at the game's official page for its requirements. If you play on a basic phone, our guide to free games for low-end Android phones shows how to pick safe ones.

Does joining a club guarantee a place at a big event?

No. The Esports World Cup Foundation says all clubs and athletes must qualify on their own merits for each title.

What to do next

  1. Choose one game and read the official rules of its events.
  2. Check the game's age rating on its official page.
  3. Look up the IESF site and read its pages for members.
  4. Keep up your school work, sleep and meals. A good routine helps you in games and in life.

Wanting to be good at something is a fine goal. Take it one step at a time, and keep your feet on solid ground.

Sources and further reading

  • About the International Esports Federation, IESF
  • International Esports Federation adds five member federations, Esports Advocate
  • KPMG: Africa's game industry earns less than 1% of $187bn global revenue, ThisDay
  • 30 top esports clubs join the Club Support Program, Esports World Cup Foundation

item.title: How Tanganyika and Zanzibar Became Tanzania in 1964
item.dc:creator: Mclean Mbaga
item.description: A calm, sourced account of how Tanganyika and Zanzibar joined in April 1964, what each source says, where they differ, and what the Union created.
item.content:encoded:
Tanzania is made of two parts that were once separate countries. Many people know the date, 26 April 1964, but fewer know how the Union came about. This post tells the story in order, says where sources differ, and takes no side in the debates people still have.

The short answer

Tanganyika became independent in December 1961, and Zanzibar in December 1963. In January 1964 a revolution changed Zanzibar's government. On 26 April 1964, Tanganyika and Zanzibar joined to form one state. It was first called the United Republic of Tanganyika and Zanzibar, and later renamed Tanzania.

  • Julius Nyerere led Tanganyika, and Abeid Karume led Zanzibar's revolutionary council.
  • The talks were kept secret.
  • Sources differ on the exact signing and approval steps.
  • The new name, Tanzania, was adopted on 29 October 1964, according to the sources we checked.

Two countries, two paths

Tanganyika became independent from Britain on 9 December 1961. You can read that story in our post on how Tanganyika won independence.

Zanzibar followed. Wikipedia's article on the Union says Zanzibar became independent from the United Kingdom on 10 December 1963 as a constitutional monarchy under its Sultan. EBSCO says Britain had set 10 December as the target date.

EBSCO also reports that in the July 1963 elections the Afro-Shirazi Party won 55 percent of the vote, while the Zanzibar Nationalist Party won a majority of seats. Mohammed Shamte became prime minister.

January 1964: the Zanzibar Revolution

On 12 January 1964, EBSCO says, a revolution broke out in Zanzibar. John Okello led it, and Abdul Rahman Mohammed Babu was a second leader. The Sultan fled, and the cabinet resigned the next day. A revolutionary council of 31 members was formed, chaired by Abeid Amani Karume.

The revolution was violent. Wikipedia says Arab and Indian people were killed in large numbers. The number of dead is disputed, and we do not give one. We mention it because a fair account must not hide it.

EBSCO also says that on 20 January 1964 a rifle corps in Tanganyika mutinied. Nyerere went into hiding until British troops from Kenya restored order. So Tanganyika's own government faced a serious test in the same weeks.

April 1964: Nyerere, Karume and the Articles of Union

EBSCO says Nyerere met the leaders of Kenya and Uganda in Nairobi on 10 and 11 April 1964 to discuss a wider federation. When he suggested including Zanzibar, they refused.

On 23 April 1964, EBSCO says, Nyerere and Karume announced a political union between Tanganyika and Zanzibar. It says the talks had been secret. Negotiators from both sides met, and Roland Brown drafted the articles.

Pius Msekwa was the Clerk of Tanganyika's Parliament at the time. The Citizen newspaper reports his account, given at a Dodoma symposium on the Union's 58th anniversary. He said Nyerere and Karume kept talks secret to avoid sabotage. He said Nyerere's trip to Zanzibar for the signing was described publicly as a friendly tour, and the truth came out that evening in a short State House statement.

What are the dates?

Here the sources differ, and we show you how.

SourceWhat it says
EBSCOAnnounced 23 April 1964. Ratified by Tanganyika's national assembly and Zanzibar's revolutionary council on 26 April 1964
Pius Msekwa, in The CitizenParliament approved at an emergency sitting on 25 April, and the Union took effect the next day
Wikipedia, Union articleUnion formed on 26 April 1964

All three agree on 26 April 1964 as the day of the Union. They differ on the steps just before it, and we have not found a source that settles who signed what and where. Msekwa's article also gives two timings for when the Union took effect, so it is best to treat that detail as unsettled.

What changed? A new state, a new name and Union matters

A new state. EBSCO says Nyerere became president of the new republic. Karume became first vice president and kept the title President of Zanzibar. Rashidi Kawawa became second vice president.

Union matters. Msekwa says the Articles of Union listed 11 Union affairs. These are subjects handled by the Union government, while others stay with each side. His article is unclear on whether the list was later enlarged. Wikipedia says Zanzibar's government kept considerable local autonomy.

An interim constitution. According to Msekwa, Tanganyika's constitution became the interim constitution of the Union, with changes that recognised Zanzibar's government and gave Zanzibar seats in the Union Parliament. It was meant to last one year.

A new name. EBSCO and Wikipedia both say the name changed to the United Republic of Tanzania on 29 October 1964. The name joins "Tanganyika" and "Zanzibar". EBSCO adds that a blue stripe was added to the flag to stand for Zanzibar. We did not find a government page for this date, so please check one if you need it for an exam or official use.

What do people still debate?

We keep this section to facts and do not say who is right.

Why did it happen? EBSCO reads the Union as a response to a crisis. In its view, it limited communist influence in Zanzibar without pushing Zanzibar into the Western camp, and it says the issue was "settled without a shot fired." That is one historian's interpretation. Others may weigh the reasons differently.

The secrecy. EBSCO says British and American diplomats learned of the Union at the last minute. Some people ask what the secrecy means for how the Union is seen. That is a matter of opinion.

The structure. Wikipedia says that in 1990 a Zanzibari coalition demanded a referendum on independence, citing the Union's economic effects, and that the demand was ignored. Debates about how the two governments share power continue. We do not offer a view on whether the arrangement should stay as it is or change.

Union Day on 26 April

Tanzanians mark 26 April as Union Day. The Citizen's report on Msekwa's talk is from a symposium held in Dodoma to mark 58 years of the Union. We have not checked an official page on whether it is a public holiday, so please check the government calendar.

Common questions

When did Tanganyika and Zanzibar unite?

On 26 April 1964, according to the sources we checked.

When did the name Tanzania start?

The sources we checked say 29 October 1964. Before that, the state was called the United Republic of Tanganyika and Zanzibar.

Who were the leaders?

Julius Nyerere of Tanganyika became president. Abeid Karume of Zanzibar became first vice president.

How many Union matters are there?

Msekwa's account lists 11 at the start. Sources differ on later changes, so check a current official source for today's list.

What to do next

  1. Learn the order: December 1961, December 1963, January 1964, April 1964, October 1964.
  2. Read the EBSCO and Citizen pieces side by side and note where they differ.
  3. For the present list of Union matters, use the Constitution or an official government page, not a summary.

Seeing both the agreed facts and the open questions is the best way to understand a shared history.
